articles.title: Beyoncé Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘You Were the Barometer’
articles.summary: Beyoncé has paid tribute to country icon Dolly Parton, who died on August 25, calling her “the barometer” and thanking her for the impact she had on the worl...
articles.body:
Beyoncé has paid tribute to country icon Dolly Parton , who died on August 25, calling her "the barometer" and thanking her for the impact she had on the world.

In a statement posted to her website , Beyoncé wrote, "Dolly, you were the barometer. The north star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship. I'm honored that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully."

Dolly Parton, 1946-2026, In Appreciation: A Life of Many Colors

Dolly Parton Tribute Specials Set on CBS, CMT

Dolly Parton's Musical Will Still Open on Broadway 'As Was Dolly's Wish'

Beyoncé had worked with Parton and recorded a reworked cover of "Jolene" for her 2024 album "Cowboy Carter," altering the original's lyrics and song structure. Where Parton begged and pleaded a woman not to steal her man on the original "Jolene," Beyoncé transformed the tune into a warning shot: "I can easily understand why you're attracted to my man / But you don't want this smoke, so shoot your shot for someone else," she sang.

Parton had hinted weeks before "Cowboy Carter" that Beyoncé had recorded her own version of "Jolene," and following the album's release, Parton took to social media to give the cover a stamp of approval. "Wow, I just heard Jolene," she wrote on social media. "Beyoncé is giving that girl some trouble and she deserves it!"

Parton's participation in "Cowboy Carter" didn't end there, as she appeared on the album with two cameos. She introduced the song "Tyrant" and had her own "Dolly P" interlude just before "Jolene." "Hey miss Honey B, it's Dolly P. You know that hussy with the good hair you sing about?" she said on "Dolly P," referencing Beyoncé's 2016 song "Sorry" and the line "Becky with the good hair." "Reminding me of someone I knew back when, except she has flaming locks of auburn hair, bless her heart. Just a hair of a different color but it hurts just the same."

She had previously supported Beyoncé recording a country album on social media, shortly after the pop star became the first Black woman to top Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart when "Texas Hold 'Em" debuted at No. 1. "I'm a big fan of Beyoncé and very excited that she's done a country album," she wrote. "So congratulations on your Billboard Hot Country number one single. Can't wait to hear the full album!"

articles.title: What to Know About Simon Cowell’s 2020 Bike Accident and Why He’s Undergoing Back Surgery Again
articles.summary: Simon Cowell broke his back in 2020 after falling off an electric bike
articles.body:
Simon Cowell fell off an electric bike in 2020 and broke his back

He was rushed to the hospital and underwent a five-hour surgery

In August 2026, Cowell's rep said the America's Got Talent judge would miss a few weeks of filming season 21 to undergo another surgery

Simon Cowell nearly lost his ability to walk six years ago.

The longtime America's Got Talent judge fell off an electric bike in the summer of 2020 and broke his back. He was taken to the hospital, where doctors told him he was "lucky" his injuries weren't worse, a source told PEOPLE at the time. Cowell then underwent a five-hour surgery to repair the damage.

"I knew I'd broken my back the minute I landed. It was really, really kind of sudden and it hurt," the former American Idol judge told Extra in February 2021. "It could have been a lot worse. When I saw the X-ray, I really nearly could have smashed my spine to pieces, so I literally wouldn't have been able to walk."

Now, six years later, Cowell is taking time off from America's Got Talent to undergo another back surgery . His rep told Entertainment Weekly that the procedure is "routine."

Here's everything to know about Simon Cowell's 2020 bike accident — and his health today.

Cowell broke his back in a 2020 bike accident

In August 2020, Cowell was at his Malibu home testing out a new e-bike when he fell and broke his back.

"Some good advice ... If you buy an electric trail bike, read the manual before you ride it for the first time. I have broken part of my back," he shared on Instagram a day later. "Thank you to everyone for your kind messages."

During a June 2021 appearance on The Kelly Clarkson Show , Cowell recalled how quickly the accident unfolded.

"In a weird way, it was kind of meant to happen because I was really pushing my luck. I was buying these crazy, crazy bikes and this particular bike I bought had so much power, I was thrown about eight feet in the air, landed on my back," he said, adding that his son, Eric , witnessed the accident.

"I knew I'd broken my back in that second, and somehow managed to get back into my bedroom," Cowell continued. "I'm lying in my bed, and covered in blood, waiting for the ambulance."

He stepped away from America's Got Talent to recover after surgery

Cowell underwent a five-hour surgery to repair his back. At the time, a source told PEOPLE that he "had to have a number of fusions and a metal rod put into his back."

The TV personality later told Extra that he was nervous about returning home from the hospital, mainly because he worried about how his son might react to seeing him in pain.

"I said, 'Lauren, I just don't know how to explain it to Eric.' She obviously said something to him because he came in … and I was lying in bed, and he said, 'Daddy, you're like Ironman,' and I thought that was the sweetest thing and it meant a lot," he recalled of a conversation with his fiancée, Lauren Silverman .

Cowell's accident came in the middle of America's Got Talent season 15, after he had already filmed the audition rounds. He stepped away from the show to recover, missing the live shows that began just days after his accident.

As he recuperated, an insider told PEOPLE in September 2020 that Cowell was " swimming many times a day to build the strength in his back." Along with doing laps and sticking to a clean diet, he also incorporated plenty of walking into his recovery.

"Being able to do things like swimming and taking long walks is big steps forward after an injury like this, but he's doing really great," the source added. "Whenever someone visits, he basically seems to want to race them on a long walk in the garden."

Cowell said he was "lucky to survive" the accident

In April 2022, Cowell spoke with OK! magazine and admitted that he had initially downplayed the severity of his accident. He also said he was "lucky to survive" his back surgery.

"It was a lot worse than people thought. I had a lot of long-term nerve damage as well," he added.

Cowell said his recovery was a long process. At one point, after he thought his bones had healed, he experienced significant pain while trying to play soccer with his son. Then, in February 2022, he suffered another setback when he fell off an e-bike in London and broke his arm .

Despite his two accidents, Cowell hasn't given up riding e-bikes.

"I'm still gonna stay on my bike. I'm obsessed with these things," he told Today in 2023.

He's taking a leave from AGT season 21 for another back surgery

In August 2026, TMZ and Entertainment Weekly reported that Cowell will temporarily step away from America's Got Talent season 21 to undergo another back surgery.

"Obviously, medical matters are private, but it's routine, and he will be back in a few weeks," a rep for Cowell told EW .

Guest judges are expected to fill in for Cowell during his absence, though no replacements have officially been announced.

articles.title: Dolly Parton Died After a ‘Brief Battle with Cancer,’ Her Team Confirms
articles.summary: The country music legend died at 80 on Tuesday, Aug. 25
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's cause of death has been revealed

Her nephew Bryan Seaver announced her death in an Instagram video on Tuesday, Aug. 25

Parton acknowledged her health struggles just days before her passing but expressed her determination to keep working

Dolly Parton 's official cause of death has been determined.

In a statement to PEOPLE on Tuesday, Aug. 25, reps for the country star confirmed the "Jolene" singer died after being diagnosed with cancer.

"Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand," the statement read.

"Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly's unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact. After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the statement concluded.

Parton died at 80 on Aug. 25 . Her nephew, Bryan Seaver, announced the news in an Instagram video the same day.

Parton was admitted to a Nashville-area hospital on Friday, Aug. 21, where she died four days later.

In his Instagram video to share the news of Parton's death, Seaver began by introducing himself.

"My name is Bryan Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I'm representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he says in the video.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he continued. "As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven't truly felt it until now."

Seaver added: "It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens."

On Friday, Aug. 21, just four days before her death, Parton herself acknowledged her recent health decline .

"As I've shared in video messages throughout the past year, I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn't pay attention to when I was watching over [my husband] Carl. You know, this isn't the first time I've had to manage something like this. Back in the early '80s, I was down for several months with female issues, and I was struggling with my weight at the time too, so it's not like I haven't been through hard times with my health," Parton told PEOPLE.

She added: "But I think because we live in a 24/7 world with social media, everything gets magnified in ways it wasn't years ago. I used to joke that I was the Queen of the Tabloids, but now I guess I can say I'm the Queen of Social Media AI! Seriously, though, even though I'm still healin', I'm still workin'! You know me — as I've often said — I've dreamed myself into a corner and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I'm gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life."

With a distinguished career that lasted decades, Parton is the best-selling female country music artist of all time, having sold more than 160 million albums worldwide. Her debut album was 1967's Hello, I'm Dolly , and she went on to release a slew of hits, including "I Will Always Love You," "9 to 5" and "Jolene."

Parton was pre-deceased by her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean , in March of 2025.

At the time, Parton announced his death on Instagram, writing, "Carl and I spent many wonderful years together. Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years."

During their long marriage, Dean opted to stay out of the spotlight but encouraged his wife. "He's always supporting me as long as I don't try to drag him in on it," Parton once told PEOPLE . "He's always been my biggest fan behind the scenes, but he's at home. I don't think they're probably showing much of this on TV, and if they do, he might see it."

"I always joke and laugh when people ask me what's the key to my long marriage and lasting love," Parton also told PEOPLE in 2018. "I always say 'Stay gone!' and there's a lot of truth to that. I travel a lot, but we really enjoy each other when we're together and the little things we do."

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Dollywood fate revealed after Queen of Country’s death
articles.summary: Parton’s namesake theme park is in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee
articles.body:
The show must go on. That's the motto that Dolly Parton's namesake theme park is abiding by in the wake of the country music legend's death .

Parton's death was announced Tuesday by her nephew in a video shared to her official Instagram account. A cause of death has not been revealed.

Dollywood, located in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, will remain open this week despite the singer's death at age 80. Parton took over as co-owner and rebranded the park as Dollywood in 1986.

Dollywood confirmed to The Independent that the park "will open as scheduled this week" and that plans for a memorial to Parton will be announced, "in the near future."

In a statement shared on Instagram , a spokesperson for Dollywood said, "With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the passing of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton . Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly's warmth, wisdom and generous spirit.

"Dolly's heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness—a space where families and friends could honor her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams," the statement continued.

"Dolly's enduring legacy extends beyond her music and generosity to her remarkable work ethic—an inspiration to people everywhere. In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted , always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle -- 'the show must go on.' Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance, and hope."

Eugene Naughton, Dollywood Parks & Resorts President, added: "The greatest privilege of my life has been helping Dolly bring her dreams to life at Dollywood. Dolly's heart was as vast as the mountains she cherished, and her compassion knew no bounds. She inspired generations to dream boldly and love deeply. While we grieve her loss, we are honored and committed to carry her light forward. Her legacy will continue to shine in every melody sung, every smile shared and every dream kindled within these gates."

The Independent has reached out to Dollywood for more information.

Parton was born in a two-room log cabin and rose to become the world's wealthiest country music star with timeless hits including "9 to 5" and "Jolene."

Her death was announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, who said: "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago."

"Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus," said Seaver, who served as Parton's head of security for more than two decades.

Within hours of Parton's death, hundreds of celebrities and politicians have paid tribute to the Queen of Country, including Donald Trump, who ordered flags to be lowered for a week following Parton's death.

articles.title: Remember This Banger: Pedro Infante's 'Cien Años' is out of this world
articles.summary: One writer's quest, with the help of notable singer-songwriters, to understand what makes Pedro Infante's "Cien Años" feel otherworldly.
articles.body:
I still remember the moment when I heard "Cien Años" for the first time. I can vividly recall the haunting aftertaste, the glorious specificity of the experience.

I had moved from Buenos Aires to Los Angeles, and somehow managed to make a living writing about Latin music. I'd seen Los Tigres del Norte in concert, shared a lengthy conversation with Vicente Fernández outside the Arrowhead Pond of Anaheim, and spent months poring through the songbook of José Alfredo Jiménez. But listening to the 1953 recording of "Cien Años" by Mexican legend Pedro Infante was a game changer — an existential milestone that will stay with me for the rest of my life.

I was in my home office, researching a story about the golden era of Mexican music. "Cien Años" played on, the elusive contours of its melody floating in the afternoon air. Three minutes and 33 seconds later, when it ended, you could hear a pin drop. I sat still for a few minutes, transfixed. Then I played it again. And again. Ten, 15, 20 times in a row.

A composition by Rubén Fuentes and Alberto Cervantes, the song wasn't just another lilting ranchera from the 1950s — that much was clear. On the contrary, it felt like an otherworldly manifestation from the gods above, as if a UFO had landed in the Mexican capital decades ago, and an advanced race of extraterrestrials left this artifact behind as some sort of exquisite offering — a reminder of everything that could be but wasn't.

There's the matter of that sinuous electric guitar intro, halfway between tropical psychedelia and merry-go-round anthem. Then, the main melody: forlorn, hallucinogenic. Infante's aristocratic delivery collides head on with the brutal indifference of the girl he will carry on loving for the rest of his embittered existence. His voice, so soft and fragile, could belong to both man and woman; the universal scar of romantic rejection.

Clearly there was a mystery attached to this evergreen standard that people got to see on the big screen in 1954, when Infante performed it in the film "Cuidado Con El Amor." The song also reminded me of Schubert — maybe a page off "Winterreise," the romantic song cycle composed in 1827.

Had I accidentally discovered a supernatural portal where time and space didn't exist, one where random phenomena of blinding beauty could materialize on this plane without any logical explanation?

To figure out why "Cien Años" still resonates, I decided to consult with a few notable singer-songwriters.

First I thought of Spanish rock star and longtime Los Angeles resident Enrique Bunbury, who himself traffics in the diffuse territories of the ominous and esoteric. I sent him a rambling voice memo, trying to convey my bewilderment as best as I could. True to his character, he replied with a terse but eloquent text.

"I apologize for the delay in responding, as I was busy promoting my new album," he wrote. "I have to agree that Pedro Infante's version has an incredibly evocative air to it that is not common in rancheras. This may be related to the classical violin training of Rubén Fuentes, who was also an arranger. Alberto Cervantes, on the other hand, was a bolero guy. I imagine he contributed the intense Acapulco scent that emanates from this song. I'm so sorry that my ignorance on this subject will probably not be of great help in your inquiry."

I marveled at Bunbury's humility, but agreed with him that the mystery was far from solved.

Maybe a young Mexican singer could shed some illumination, I thought, before sending a somewhat incoherent email to Silvana Estrada. I was right to assume that the 29-year-old prodigy behind 2025's "Vendrán Suaves Lluvias" — one of the most spiritually devastating albums of the decade, and the second best album of last year — would have something to say.

"This is one of the most gorgeous boleros in the Mexican repertoire," Estrada replied.

"I always thought the Pedro Infante version was mind-boggling. There is something in the string arrangement that sounds a bit impressionistic to me, but also profoundly Mexican, with the trumpets doubling the violin lines. There's also a sense of maximalism that sums up the old Mexico as a time of splendor. And when I think of this song, I think of something splendid."

At least now I knew that I was not alone in my overwhelming passion for this strange little gem. But neither Bunbury nor Estrada had addressed the eerie supernatural vibe that emanates from the recording — the feeling that when "Cien Años" was recorded somewhere in Mexico City, Pedro and company connected with another dimension.

I was scheduled to interview Mexican American singer Lila Downs the following day, and I decided to bring this up at the end of our chat. She was sitting down in her stately Oaxaca home when we connected over Zoom, and smiled widely the moment I brought up my metaphysical query.

"I've experienced a similar feeling with other songs that I've performed," she said. "It's like they transport me to a más allá [a far beyond], a certain undefined something that doesn't belong in my own era. 'La Llorona,' in fact, connects me to something that is not even human — a force that exists in the shape of waves. It's the essence of the very mystery that music itself evokes in all of us."

Downs pointed out an important detail: that "Cien Años" could not have emerged from any country other than Mexico.

"Our subconscious is loaded with the spirit of the ancestors," she added. "There is a deep connection with the cosmos in Mexico. I've seen it in anthropology books; this vision of art as a healing agent that facilitates spiritual growth."

I was finally ready to put the matter aside, when I spoke to Gepe. The Chilean singer-songwriter has crafted many tracks that have a timeless, soulful quality to them. "Desastre," a lovely tune released in 2024, feels almost as unearthly to me as "Cien Años."

"That intro is definitely striking," he told me in the first of many voice memos. "It has a psychedelic tinge that didn't really exist in the 1950s. It reminds me of someone like Peter Drake and his slide guitar playing, which had more of a Hawaiian sound. I think it's beautiful that such a short intro can leave you with more questions than answers. That's part of the magic, isn't it?"

Gepe made an astute observation: that my life-changing experience with "Cien Años" was not due to a single factor. It was a layered, complex combination of different details.

"You have this incredible, hypersensitive performance by Pedro, coupled with a timeless arrangement which was definitely ahead of its time," he explained. "The cinematic, almost Hawaiian touch on the guitar, but also a strong affinity to the bolero aesthetic — there's a subtle softness in the maracas, so that the voice can grow and shine with so much sweetness."

And then, he told me the one thing that brought it all together.

"It's funny, because you keep saying that this song sounds like it landed from another world, but there's a stark contradiction in that statement," he said. "Pedro's delivery is so marvelous and sensitive, that it goes beyond male or female — it sums up the human experience in all its subtlety and aching beauty. I think what happened here was that the composers, arrangers, musicians and Pedro got together in a studio and created something so immense and luminous that it ended up transcending its own sense of time."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Blake Shelton, Reba McEntire, Kacey Musgraves and More Country Stars Pay Tribute to Dolly Parton After Death at 80
articles.summary: PEOPLE confirmed Parton died on Tuesday, Aug. 25
articles.body:
Country stars shared heartfelt tributes after Dolly Parton died on Tuesday, Aug. 25

In the tributes, the singers reflected on Dolly Parton's kindness, influence, and legacy in music and beyond

Many artists, including Maren Morris and Trace Adkins, highlighted her generosity and impact on their personal and professional lives

The country community is mourning the death of their beloved Dolly Parton .

Moments after the news broke that the Queen of Country died in Nashville on Tuesday, Aug. 25, at age 80, fellow country artists flooded social media with heartfelt tributes.

Blake Shelton shared a photo from Parton's appearance on The Voice and expressed his heartbreak at hearing the news.

"I can say with absolute certainty that we are all feeling the same heart brokenness today," Shelton wrote on Instagram . "I only got to spend any real time with Dolly when Gwen and I got to work with her on The Voice. I want everyone to know that she was the EXACT person that you think she is. It was like being with the funnest, most loving, most caring and closest member of your family. Truly a loss for the entire world. We love you Dolly."

Parton's longtime friend Reba McEntire shared photos of them together over the years — and began her caption by writing that she had just gotten the news that her "buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side."

"Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart," she wrote on Instagram . "There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang. Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She's gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her. I'll never forget the first time I met you and I'll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba."

On his Instagram Stories , Keith Urban wrote that he was "heartbroken" over the news.

"Honestly," he began, "I have no words right now."

Kacey Musgraves kept it simple on X and shared her name with a broken heart emoji, alongside "this really really hurts."

"The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden," she wrote in a follow-up post , adding, "So glad she's with her Carl Dean . No one talk to me today."

Singer-songwriter Natalie Hemby shared photos from a performance with The Highwomen and Parton, whom she called her "Tennessee hero."

"I just wanna thank @amandapearlshires @marenmorris @brandicarlile for asking me to be in @thehighwomen … one of the many reasons being that I got to meet my Tennessee hero, and sing with her, and tell her how much she meant to me, and thank her for her songs and for being an example of how to love people," she wrote on Instagram . "I will always love you, Dolly. Thank you for all the joy that you brought to this world. You will forever live on in the music…and in my heart!"

The Band Perry's Kimberly Perry shared a sweet story on Instagram about the time producer Rick Rubin gave Parton her phone number.

"He wanted her to talk some courage into me. And she did - she called me herself, this gorgeous soul, my fellow East Tennessean, and told me to be bold with my voice. It's one of the most iconic, turning-point moments of my life," she wrote. "Years later, I got to sing her favorite song of mine - 'I Will Always Love You' - at the White House. Full circle doesn't even cover it. Heartbroken doesn't even come close. She is my hero. My queen. There will never be another her. Fly high, Mrs. Dolly. Fly high. 🕊️"

Jo Dee Messina shared a video of herself singing "I Will Always Love You" — which was written by Parton and famously performed later by Whitney Houston — and wrote, "We will always love you" over the clip.

"There are no words to ease the sadness. Dolly, I remember being a little girl and learning every single one of your songs. My parents had your records, and I would listen to them endlessly," she captioned her video. "You've made a way for so many of us. Thank you for that! You were always the brightest light in the room. You will be greatly missed. I love you 💔"

Maren Morris shared a throwback Instagram video of Parton singing alongside her — and she wrote in the caption that there will "never be another" Parton.

"[Parton] was who we could all agree on. she was and is such a light. 💔" wrote Morris.

Ty Herndon wrote that country music "lost one of its most legendary artists and trailblazers."

"Words aren't enough at a time like this to encapsulate everything @dollyparton meant to me and the entire planet. We will always love you, Dolly! 🦋" Herndon wrote alongside a throwback photo with Parton on Instagram .

John Carter Cash shared a sweet childhood photo with Parton and sent love to her family in the caption.

"Her music, of course, influenced multiple generations all around the world. But her heart and giving love for humanity overshadowed even her music. Blessings to the legacy of the lady…" Cash wrote.

Jennifer Nettles posted a black-and-white image of Parton and said the world was a "much better place" because of her.

"She was a singing, dazzling, rhinestone example of what it means to be giving, kind, generous, gracious, and loving. She leaves us an artistic legacy that will never even remotely be rivaled, and moreover, she showed us what it means to be a leader of culture and an ally to those who need it most," Nettles wrote on Instagram . "And she did it all with a twinkle in her eye. Our hearts are broken at losing such a light. The stars will sparkle brighter tonight with her spirit. Thank you Dolly. For everything."

Chris Janson , who collaborated with Parton on "21 Forever," shared a photo performing alongside Parton on Instagram and wished for her to "rest in heaven."

"Dolly was a wonderful person, and it stopped me in my tracks hearing of her passing. TRUE ICON, TRUE STAR, and REAL GREAT HUMAN. We'll always love you, Dolly. My family is grateful the time we got to spend alongside of you. Love, CJ" he wrote.

Trace Adkins acknowledged that it was "rare for the world" to collectively "express sorrow for someone's passing."

"I knew her to be the angel that they think she was, and I'll miss her. Dolly, I'll always love you. -Trace" he wrote on Instagram .

Gabby Barrett reflected on her first time meeting Parton in an Instagram post — and she remembered hugging her "a little too hard" because she was so excited.

"I got to pick her brain some about this business and was lucky enough to receive encouragement from her along the way. She sent me a handwritten card with butterflies on it, and I know exactly where that card is in my house. I made a point to keep it forever, and I always will," Barrett wrote.

"And crazy enough, Baylah (my 5 year old) just recently asked me, 'Mom, when am I gonna get to meet Dolly Parton?' I told her, 'Hmmm I'm not sure.' There was just nobody like her. She was so witty and could make you laugh, and then turn around and break your heart with a song," she concluded. "She was a songwriter and a country music woman through and through. I don't know if I've ever seen someone so dedicated to this music and to what it means. She gave so much to country music, but I'll always be especially grateful for the little bit of kindness and encouragement she gave to me. A true treasure who will be missed."

Georgette Jones , the daughter of the late George Jones and Tammy Wynette, wrote that her family was "very sad" to hear of Parton's passing on Instagram .

"She was incredibly talented....as we all know, but she was also a generous, kind and wonderful friend to Mom, Dad and so many others," she wrote. "She gave so much of herself to help people and children, especially, in need. She will be dearly missed."

The Rascal Flatts' Jay DeMarcus shared a photo with Parton and began by writing he had "no words."

"There was not a kinder, more genuine, loving person than Ms Dolly," he wrote on Instagram . "What an unbelievable loss, I kinda thought she'd be here forever I guess. Now she's singing with the other Angels…"

Dasha reshared a post of Parton on her Instagram Stories — and wrote she was "devastated."

"Dolly thank you for inspiring me and so many others. You've done so much good for this world. RIP you legend," she continued.

Tiera Kennedy shared a photo alongside Parton on Instagram and simply wrote, "Oh Dolly. We will always love you. ♥️."

Terri Clark wrote that in losing Parton, country music lost its "matriarch" — and that she was "so much more than an entertainer."

"She swung the pendulum toward the light in times of darkness. She gave back so much more than she ever took and used her name and influence for the greater good. THAT'S WHY the song 'What Would Dolly Do' was written and loved," Clark wrote on Instagram .

"The world almost feels off its axis right now, and how we exist in it without her remains to be seen. She taught us so much through her heart and her actions and left behind a legacy of love and light. Now she is in that light with her loved ones and her God. Thank you, Dolly, for inspiration beyond music. Humanity is better because of you," she continued.

Connie Smith shared two side-by-side photos with Parton over the years on Instagram .

"God bless you, Dolly. We have always loved and will continue to love you dearly. ❤️," she wrote.

articles.title: A nosy polar bear and a lucky squirrel: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 shortlist
articles.summary: The polar bear image taken by Audun Rikardsen was among the 'highly commended' entries in this year's competition.
articles.body:
How would it feel to find yourself face to face with one of the Arctic's most formidable predators?

This stunning image captures life from a seal's perspective. Taken by Norwegian wildlife photographer Audun Rikardsen, it was among the 'Highly Commended' entries in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

While working as a guide with Arctic Wildlife Tours, Rikardsen rigged an underwater camera with a motion sensor beneath a seal's breathing hole, and then waited. At 4am, a female polar bear approached and peered down.

Rikardsen then waited eight hours for the bear to move away before retrieving the camera and reviewing the images.

When he saw what he had captured, he said: "I was so extremely happy. I was screaming, so I probably woke up all the polar bears for miles."

Rikardsen has previously won two Wildlife Photographer of the Year categories: Birds in 2019 and Oceans: The Bigger Picture in 2025 .

The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London from Friday 16 October 2026.

Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition.

Living alongside polar bears in the Canadian Arctic - BBC World Service

Crockford watched swifts return to London after their annual migration from Africa, filling the air with their high-pitched calls. Most flew too high to photograph, but a few lower-flying ones gave Crockford the opportunity to capture the picture he wanted.

Swifts spend almost their entire lives in the air, usually landing only to nest.

After rainfall, Miyazawa came across an Eastern Japanese toad making its way along a city street. He used a slow shutter speed to photograph it before it hopped back into the bushes.

Eastern Japanese toads are typically found in forests, grasslands and other terrestrial habitats across eastern Japan, but they have also proved remarkably adaptable to urban environments.

Photographer: Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen (Norway)

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Mammals

Location: Kvænangen, Troms County, Norway

Aasen was flying a drone for the Norwegian Orca Survey when he noticed an adult orca carrying the body of a deceased calf through a Norwegian fjord.

The orca repeatedly allowed the calf to sink before bringing it back to the surface, a difficult moment to watch but one that Aasen felt was important to record.

The behaviour may have been an attempt to revive or protect the calf. Killer whales have previously been observed carrying deceased calves, including a case where a female Southern Resident killer whale carried her dead calf for at least 17 days.

A 2026 study suggests that this type of behaviour may be more widespread across the species than previously thought.

Photographer: Andrea & Maceo Grammatico (France)

Category: Highly Commended, Animal Portraits

Location: Sierpe, South Puntarenas, Costa Rica

Only when they reviewed the images did the Grammatico twins realise they had captured a mosquito resting on the head of a fer-de-lance viper. They described it as "one of the most demanding focus stacks we've ever created".

Highly venomous and responsible for more fatal snake bites in Central America than any other species, the fer-de-lance is well camouflaged and can blend into plantation habitats, sometimes going unnoticed by workers.

Location: Meeting of the Waters State Park, Northern Pantanal, Brazil

Parkinson photographed a black vulture perched over a dead yacaré caiman in Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, keeping his boat at a distance and using a long telephoto lens to capture the shot.

A jaguar waiting out of frame emerged after the vulture flew away to claim the carcass. Only then did Parkinson notice a suspiciously clean, straight wound on the back of the caiman's head, possibly caused by a blow from a speeding boat, he suspects.

Photographer: Dewald Tromp (South Africa)

Category: Highly Commended, Animals in their Environment

Location: Namib Desert, near Swakopmund, Namibia

Tromp was photographing a Namaqua chameleon in the Namib Desert when the wind suddenly intensified, bringing a sandstorm that quickly reduced visibility and made breathing difficult.

These chameleons are desert specialists and can obtain moisture directly from the air. Dew gathers on their skin and is channelled towards their mouths through microscopic grooves, while their tongues can also collect fog water condensed on plants, sand and rocks.

Photographer: Bence Máté (Hungary) - 2010 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Birds

Location: Ashnil Aruba Lodge, Tsavo East National Park, Kenya

Máté was watching birds gather at a small pond when tens of thousands of red-billed queleas swept down to drink in the golden late-afternoon light. The movement of so many wings created a rush of air that, he says, could be felt from 30m (98ft) away.

Red-billed queleas can gather in flocks of up to two million and are considered the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with an estimated 1.5 billion breeding adults.

Photographer: Ernest Porter (South Africa)

Location: Manyeleti Game Reserve, Mpumalanga, South Africa

While searching the reserve for wildlife, Porter photographed a red-billed oxpecker rubbing its bill against a white rhino's skin in the afternoon light. The birds feed on insects living on rhinos and can also act as sentinels - calling to warn their hosts when danger approaches. In Swahili, the red-billed oxpecker is known as askari wa kifaru, meaning "the rhino's guard".

Hutton had watched a young leopard pursue a squirrel into a tree, having earlier seen the cat unsuccessfully attempt to stalk a rabbit. The squirrel escaped by climbing higher, leaving the leopard clinging on before it eventually made an awkward retreat.

For young leopards, survival is far from guaranteed: fewer than half reach independence, with male leopards, lions and other predators among the threats they face.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles

Location: Central Kalahari Game Reserve, Botswana

An African bullfrog lunges for a babul butterfly but misses.

Cullmann had noticed tadpoles on a previous visit after heavy rains and returned the following month to find ponds and puddles full of young bullfrogs. He spent more than two weeks watching the young frogs "eat everything that moved".

As adults, African bullfrogs can reach 12cm (4.7in) in length and spend around 10 months of the year dormant underground, emerging after the rains to breed and feed voraciously.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Invertebrates

Location: Wildsumaco Biological Station, Napo Province, Ecuador

Wizen was photographing a lichen dragon katydid measuring just 15mm long, making it difficult to distinguish from the lichen around it. He spotted the insect when it moved, but even then struggled to separate it from its background through the viewfinder.

Found only in Ecuador's Andes Mountains, its spiny armour helps protect it from eagle-eyed predators that can see through its disguise.

Photographer: Shane Gross (Canada) - 2024 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Oceans: The Bigger Picture

Gross was photographing a school of bigeye trevally near the shore at sunrise as a storm approached. To create a split-level image, he turned his camera upside down to aid buoyancy distribution and slowly moved towards the curious fish.

Bigeye trevally are fished in many parts of the world, but here they are relatively safe. In 2023, the waters surrounding D'Arros Island were made a Marine Protected Area and designated as a no-take zone as part of the worldwide initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030.

Category: Highly Commended, Urban Wildlife

Elliott spent hours watching through the kitchen window of a local resident's home, hoping to photograph black bears that frequently pass through the garden. He observed one stopping for a dip in the garden pool, highlighting the increasingly common overlap between wildlife and residential life in Los Angeles County, where housing developments have spread into bear habitat.

Photographer: Ralph Pace (USA) - 2025 Underwater category winner

Category: Highly Commended, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture

A sea hare glides through an eelgrass meadow in the shallows of Monterey Bay, where Pace was photographing in the evening light. He saw the encounter as a hopeful image of "a gentle giant safeguarding the last green meadows of the sea".

By grazing on red algae, that can prevent sunlight reaching the meadow, sea hares play a role in restoring eelgrass, which is vital to coastal ecosystems and an important carbon sink.

Category: Highly Commended, Photojournalism

After learning that a circus featuring animal acts was in town, Rojas went to document it and saw a brown bear riding a small motorcycle, muzzled and secured to the apparatus. For him the scene highlighted the contrast between the animal's wild nature and the human environment imposed upon it.

More than 50 countries around the world have now banned or restricted the use of wild animals in circuses, over concerns it causes them distress .

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London.

articles.title: Dolly Parton dies at the age of 80: A look at her life through photos
articles.summary: Dolly Parton got her start in the entertainment industry after making her debut at the Grand Ole Opry at the age of 13. Here is a look back at her career in music, film and philanthropy.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton dies at the age of 80: A look at her life through photos Dolly Parton got her start in the entertainment industry after making her debut at the Grand Ole Opry at the age of 13. Here is a look back at her career in music, film and philanthropy. Start Slideshow

Dolly Parton got her start in the entertainment industry after making her debut at the Grand Ole Opry at the age of 13. Here is a look back at her career in music, film and philanthropy.

Born in January 1949, Dolly Parton made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry in 1959 at age 13 before moving to Nashville in 1960 to make it as a professional country singer.

Dolly Parton and Carl Thomas Dean got married in 1966.

Parton released her first solo album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in 1967, after which Porter Wagoner invited her onto "The Porter Wagoner Show."

Parton continued her partnership with Wagner throughout the early 70s, and became an official member of the Grand Ole Opry in 1969.

Parton released her fifth studio album, "The Fairest of Them All," in February 1970.

Parton released one of her most popular songs, "I Will Always Love You," in 1974, which she wrote about the end of her partnership from Porter Wagoner.

Parton launched her own variety television show, "Dolly!" in 1976, which often featured many other famous singers.

Parton released the album, "Here You Come Again" in 1976, which spent five weeks at number one on Billboard's country charts.

In 1978, Dolly Parton won her first Grammy Award for "Here You Come Again" and later won entertainer of the year at the CMA Awards.

Parton was nominated for another Academy Award and Golden Globe Award for best original song for "Travelin' Thru" for the film "Transamerica."

Parton made her feature film debut in 1980 in the hit comedy, "9-5," alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. She also wrote the films title track, an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song, two Golden Globe nominations and two Grammy Award wins.

Parton also wrote the film's title track, an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song, two Golden Globe nominations and two Grammy Award wins.

She received her another Golden Globe nomination in 1982 for her work in the movie "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas."

Parton partnered with Kenny Rogers in 1983, releasing their number 1 hit, "Islands In the Stream."

Parton opened her own theme park, Dollywood, in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, in 1976.

Parton launched a variety television show, "Dolly" in 1987, which was a major ABC prime-time series with a large production budget.

Her new show featured a Christmas episode with puppets.

She also invited the Chippendales to appear on her show with her.

Parton made light of a 1987 tabloid story that she fell in love with a 300 lb wrestler, writing the song, "He's Got a Headlock on my Heart.."

One of the many celebrity guests on her show included Bob Hope.

Parton won another Grammy Award in 1988 for best country performance by a duo or group for her work with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris.

In 1989, Parton starred in the successful film,"Steel Magnolias," alongside Julia Roberts, Shirley MacLaine, Sally Fields and Daryl Hannah.

Parton released "Eagle When She Flies" in 1991, which went on to achieve platinum status.

Whitney Houston's cover of "I Will Always Love You" spent 14 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 list, which benefitted her as a songwriter and introduced her songwriting skills to a different audience.

She also starred in "Straight Talk" in 1992, and wrote and performed much of the music for the film, including "Straight Talk," "Light of a Clear Blue Morning" and "Blue Grace."

While maintaining the responsibilities of running a theme park, she teamed up with Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette to release "Honky Tonk Angels."

Parton started the Imagination Library in 1995, which provided young children with free books mailed directly to their homes, regardless of family income. She started the program in honor of her father, who couldn't read.

By 2024, approximately 1 in every 7 U.S. children under age five was receiving a monthly Imagination Library book, with of 300 million books gifted by 2025.

1999 was a big year for Parton, as she was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and released the critically acclaimed album, "The Grass Is Blue."

Parton won her sixth Grammy Award in 2001 for "The Grass Is Blue" in the best bluegrass album, category.

Parton received both the National Medal of Arts and the Living Legend Award from the Library of Congress in 2004.

Parton received another Academy Award and Golden Globe Award nomination for best original song for her song, "Travelin' Thru" for the film "Transamerica."

Parton received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006.

Parton appeared alongside her goddaughter, Miley Cyrus, in a 2007 episode of "Hannah Montana," playing Aunt Dolly.

Parton was honored with a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2011.

Parton and Rogers reunited in 2013, for "You Can't Make Old Friends," 30 years after "Islands In the Stream."

Parton wowed the crowd when performing at Glastonbury in 2014.

Parton created the My People Fund in 2016 following wildfires in the Great Smoky Mountains, which ultimately provided about $9 million to affected families.

The singer received another Grammy and Golden Globe nomination for best original song in 2018 for "Girl in the Movies."

Parton celebrated 50 years at the Grand Ole Opry in 2019.

Parton won a Grammy for "There Was Jesus" and her first Emmy for "Christmas on the Square" in 2021 at the age of 75.

Parton was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

Parton performed at the halftime show at the Dallas Cowboys’ Thanksgiving Day game in 2023, dressed as a Dallas Cowboy Cheerleader.

After being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Parton released the album "Rockstar" in 2023 which featured, Chris Stapleton, Paul McCartney, Steven Tyler and others.

Parton was named the No. 1 country artist of all time by Billboard in 2024.

Parton sparked health concerns in 2025 when she postponed her Las Vegas residency citing health as the reason.

Parton died on August 25 at the age of 80.

articles.title: Dolly Parton, beloved country music icon, dies at 80 after 'brief battle with cancer'
articles.summary: Dolly Parton, the beloved singer, songwriter, actor and philanthropist, has died, her family said on Tuesday. She was 80 years old.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the beloved singer, songwriter, actor and philanthropist, has died, her family said on Tuesday. She was 80 years old.

In a statement issued to People , Parton's rep shared that the Queen of Country had "bravely [faced] a brief battle with cancer." She was "surrounded by loved ones" while receiving medical care at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville.

"Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched," the statement read. "Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand," the statement read.

"Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly's unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact. After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the statement concluded.

In a video statement shared to Instagram on Tuesday, Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver — the son of Cassie Parton and Parton's head of security for more than two decades — shared the news that Parton had died. He said the video announcement was something that his aunt asked him to do "years ago."

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light, and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents, and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens," he said.

While Seaver did not disclose details around Parton's death, he reflected on her legacy, which included opening doors for "generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent" and changing history.

"She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever," he continued.

"Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil. She farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

According to a post on Parton's Instagram account, "a small, private service will be held for immediate family" at the singer's request. "In lieu of flowers the family asks for donations to be made to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library at ."

President Trump on Tuesday afternoon said on social media that Parton's death "is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM. Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you."

Parton's death comes after she announced in May 2026 that she was canceling her Las Vegas residency , which was set to begin in September after already being postponed nine months. She cited unspecified health issues but told the public, via Instagram video , that she was "responding really well to meds and treatments" and "improving every day."

Known as the Queen of Country , Parton built a successful career that spanned decades, during which she became one of the most honored female country performers of all time. She received 10 Grammy Awards, plus a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and a Primetime Emmy Award, and she holds the record for a female artist with 25 No. 1s on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart.

Parton was the fourth of 12 children born to Avie Lee Caroline Owens and Robert Lee Parton Sr., on Jan. 19, 1946, and grew up in Locust Ridge, Tenn. She often credited her uncle Bill Owens for encouraging her to pursue music after buying her a guitar and getting her a role on a television variety show in Knoxville when she was 10.

After graduating from high school in 1964, Parton moved to Nashville to pursue a career in music. She met her husband, Carl Dean, on her first day in the city , at a laundromat. The two would wed in 1966 and stay married until his death on March 3, 2025.

Parton's big break came in 1967 when Porter Wagoner asked her to replace his duet partner, Norma Jean, on the syndicated TV series The Porter Wagoner Show . The Country Music Hall of Fame credits Parton's "hourglass figure, outrageous outfits, and angelic voice" for why she performed so well as Wagoner's cohost.

Parton signed with RCA Records as both a solo artist and Wagoner's partner, and her first solo No. 1 hit was "Joshua" in 1971, which led to the success of "Jolene," "Love Is Like a Butterfly" and "I Will Always Love You" in 1974. The latter song, which she wrote in honor of Wagoner after she left his show earlier that year, would go on to become a No. 1 pop hit when Whitney Houston covered it in 1992 for The Bodyguard soundtrack.

Parton herself crossed over to the pop charts with her recording of "Here You Come Again" in 1977. Her song "9 to 5" was the title song of the film of the same name and marked Parton's film debut in 1980, starring alongside Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda. The song won two Grammys and was Oscar-nominated. She starred in a number of films, including The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas with Burt Reynolds in 1982 and Steel Magnolias with Sally Field and Julia Roberts in 1989.

She also opened Dollywood — a theme park that became a significant tourist attraction and helped fund her nonprofit Dollywood Foundation, which supports local schools and scholarship programs — in East Tennessee in 1986. The foundation launched Imagination Library in 1995, and the program now mails millions of free books to children in multiple countries.

Parton was philanthropic in many ways. After the 2016 Sevier County wildfires, the My People Fund raised and distributed more than $12 million. Parton also donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, connected to COVID-19 vaccine research.

Parton would go back to her roots and record several bluegrass albums throughout the early 2000s, after being inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999. She founded her own label, Dolly Records, in 2007 and wrote the music and lyrics for the Broadway adaptation of 9 to 5 , earning her a Tony Award nomination in 2009.

The honors continued throughout her life. The Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award came in 2011, after a Kennedy Center Honors award in 2006. In 2022, she was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and in 2025 won the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

In later years, Parton dealt with health issues that forced her to pull out of public events. She didn't attend a Dollywood event in September 2025, after being diagnosed with an infection related to a kidney stone. Later that month, she announced she had to postpone her Las Vegas residency over "health challenges." In May 2026, she canceled the residency, slated for September 2026, citing undisclosed health issues and treatment that left her unable to perform.

Parton never had children of her own but is survived by several siblings and nieces and nephews. In 2014, she spoke to People about her relationship with her siblings and their kids. "I grew up in a big old family with eight kids younger than me and several of my brothers and sisters came to live with me early on in my life," she said at the time. "I've loved their kids just like they're my grandkids, and now I've got great-grand-kids!"

She added: "I often think, it just wasn't meant for me to have kids so everybody's kids can be mine."

articles.summary: Conoce todos los detalles sobre este magno evento de musica regional mexicana
articles.body: La nueva edición de Arre Pepsi Black buscará repetir el éxito que tuvo en su debut capitalino, cuando el encuentro logró convocar a más de 70 mil personas por día. Tras llevar su propuesta hasta Monterrey, el festival volverá a la Ciudad de México para reunir en un mismo escenario a grandes figuras del regional mexicano y a algunos de los exponentes que representan las nuevas generaciones del género. El regreso a la capital también marca un reencuentro con el público que acompañó al festival desde sus primeros pasos en 2023. Con una cartelera que combina nombres consolidados como Alejandro Fernández, Banda MS y Los Tucanes de Tijuana con artistas de la nueva ola, ARRE Pepsi Black apuesta nuevamente por mostrar la diversidad y evolución que atraviesa actualmente la música mexicana El Arre Pepsi Black 2026 se llevará a cabo durante dos días en la Ciudad de México: sábado 5 y domingo 6 de septiembre de 2026. El encuentro tendrá como sede el Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, donde los asistentes podrán disfrutar de una amplia selección de artistas representantes del regional mexicano. Esta nueva edición marcará el regreso del festival al recinto donde se realizaron sus primeras ediciones, por lo que los seguidores de la música mexicana podrán disfrutar nuevamente de una jornada que combinará distintos estilos y generaciones. El cartel incluye figuras como Alejandro Fernández, Banda MS y Los Tucanes de Tijuana, además de otros exponentes que completarán la programación de ambos días. articles.title: Jennifer Garner Left Los Angeles to Spend ‘a Couple of Days’ By Herself After Losing Out on “The West Wing”. She Landed “Alias ”‘2 Weeks Later’
articles.summary: The actress explains how the profession steels people against rejection
articles.body:
Jennifer Garner looked back at a role she missed out on during her recent appearance on Aspire with Emma Grede

The actress, 54, looked back at missing out on a role in The West Wing , recalling it as a rejection she took particularly hard

While Garner took the news hard, just weeks later, Alias came into play

Jennifer Garner believes that everything happens for a reason.

During an appearance on Aspire with Emma Grede , the actress, 54, opened up about handling rejection, noting that getting good at it is part of persisting as an actor.

"Do you know how many auditions or meetings I've gone on that I've gotten down to here, to here , and not gotten?" she posed.

Garner continued, "And then you do get one and you take it. It's like this big thing and you think, 'Oh great, this is going to be amazing.' You get it and you sell it with everything you have and it just lies there on the floor. And you just think, 'I loved you. I thought you were great.' "

The Five Star Weekend actress was proud to share she believes she has "good bounce" and a good ability to "shake it off." She did note that it is hard not to take such decisions personally, recalling one time she lost out on a role she really wanted.

"I always think back to this audition for The West Wing . It was for a new role and God, I wanted it so badly. And I got down and I tested for it. And when I didn't get it, I had to like, go to the desert," she admitted.

"It was my first time in Palm Springs by myself and just sit there for a couple of days. And then, like two weeks later, Alias came to me," Garner continued. "So what is it? Rejection is God's protection? Whatever that is, I'm all for that. Let's believe that, you know? Let's go with that."

The ABC spy series, created by J.J. Abrams , ran for five seasons, from September 2001 to May 2006. Garner played double agent Sydney Bristow in what became her breakthrough role. The cast also included Ron Rifkin, Victor Garber , Michael Vartan, Bradley Cooper , Merrin Dungey, Carl Lumbly, Kevin Weisman and Greg Grunberg.

In a 2026 chat with PEOPLE, Garner said she would "never forget the day we wrapped" on the series. She recalled, "We wrapped actually in April. It'll be 20 years in April. I didn't realize that because I just think about it since we aired, which is almost 25 years."

"The day before our last day was my birthday, I think, and the crew had a plane fly over with a banner for me, so I remember that. And I feel like my mom was visiting. It was very emotional," she continued.

"It was so emotional. I've never been able to watch the last episode because Victor's character dies and I just can't see it. I can't even see it," Garner admitted.

articles.title: ‘The Dog Stars’ Review: Jacob Elordi’s Sensitive Survivalist Can’t Sustain a Dreary Dystopian Adventure
articles.summary: It’s the end of the world as we know it in “The Dog Stars,” and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine? Alive, hanging in there, taking...
articles.body:
It's the end of the world as we know it in "The Dog Stars," and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine ? Alive, hanging in there, taking it one day at a time. Things could be better, which goes without saying in the aftermath of a flu pandemic that has wiped out most of the planet's human population, but the four principals here could also be dead, so there's that. That shrugging, slightly bereft air of just-getting-by is the prevailing mood of Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic survival story, and it's a tough one to sustain dramatically, much less with any sense of intrepid adventure. Somewhat aptly released at the tail end of a long, loud movie summer, this is a surprisingly low-energy, low-incident blockbuster; you'd appreciate its mellow, character-oriented approach if it gave you any real characters to hold onto.

Peter Heller's popular 2012 source novel largely did. Concentrated and eventful, it brought Jack London-style terseness and lyricism, as well as some mordant gallows humor, to the oft-solitary saga of Hig, a qualified mechanic eking out a life on an abandoned airstrip in rural Colorado, less than a decade after the fateful plague. (The year in the film is given, most pessimistically, as 2035. Start stockpiling now.) On the page, Hig's first-person descriptions of his everyday adventures, and of the waning natural world around him, had an honest, melancholy soul to them. That voice doesn't carry over to the adaptation by screenwriter Mark L. Smith — something of a specialist in survivalist drama, having also scripted "The Revenant" and "The Midnight Sky" — which forgoes narration altogether; the film bets on Jacob Elordi's blokey, slightly sad-eyed charm to fill in the gaps.

Ridley Scott Says 'I'm Not a Filmmaker, I'm an Influencer'

Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott's 'The Dog Stars' When Asked if He's Been Auditioning: 'I'm Here on Holiday'

American Independent Film Production Is Dying. Jeff Nichols Wants to Save It.

It's not a bad bet; it just doesn't quite pay off. Elordi's gift as a performer is for mining deeper seams of humanity in unappealing characters, from the douchey trust-fund scion of "Saltburn" to the literal monster of "Frankenstein." Given a simply dull one, as he is here, he fares less well. The film's Hig is nice; he's admirably practical and resourceful; he looks terrific in weathered Carhartt workwear. But even handed the sympathetic accoutrements of a faithful German shepherd sidekick and repeated silent flashbacks to his deceased wife, he remains a bit of a blank. The film's strangely lackadaisical opening act, heavy on scenes of Hig flying his battered Cessna alone, desperately needs the gruff friction provided by Josh Brolin as Bangley, his fellow survivor turned reluctant platonic life partner.

Hig and Bangley have an established routine that keeps them alive, if not all that elated to be so. Hig regularly flies to Denver, now a bombed-out ghost town, to pick up supplies from sundry abandoned stores, bars and hospitals. On their compound, they alternate guard duty, on the alert for sporadic bands of intruders, whom Bangley insists be shot on sight. When Hig can't take it anymore, desperate for any kind of escape, he winds up crash-landing his plane near the spartan farm of grizzled rancher Jack (Guy Pearce) and his lonely daughter Cima (Margaret Qualley), whose routine is similarly, joylessly focused on existence and endurance: The grass, of course, is always greener on the other side of the Rockies. A thin romance ensues. The dramatic tempo stays much the same.

At its most interesting, "The Dog Stars" mimics the structure and stakes of a classic frontier Western, echoed quite literally in its two liveliest action setpieces: a briefly spectacular yet unperilous buffalo stampede, and a faceoff with a marauding tribe of feral, thickly made-up men on horseback, rather incuriously positioned by the film as an outright enemy force. The old-fashioned cowboys-and-Indians dynamic of this sequence is hard to ignore, as is the shared whiteness of the film's leading characters: In this dog-eat-dog world, whose brutal survival strategies get to be heroic, and why?

Smith's spare, episodic script doesn't risk such introspection, or indeed much else — save for one whopper of a departure from the novel, late in the proceedings, that sharply wrests the tone from ruggedly earnest wilderness drama to macabre, borderline-camp horror-comedy, only to reverse course so abruptly you wonder if either you or the film dropped out for a quick fever-dream. It certainly yanks your attention amid the generally homey, lolloping rhythm of the film. It also more or less demolishes whatever credibility this future-rustic story world has built up to this point. In this case, Scott's famously catholic genre interests come at some cost to the integrity of the whole enterprise; you sense he might feel as impatient with these sturdy, morose, faintly drab characters as we do.

All four stars ably play the stoic and sorrowful notes required of them, without finding many secondary or contrasting ones in their dialogue. "The Dog Stars" winds up coasting on their collective capabilities and charisma, as well as on Scott's autopilot proficiency. If the tirelessly prolific director never seems more than intermittently invested in this material, the strongest passages here thrive on his muscular command of scale, and he can still pick a landscape with the best of them: Northern Italy fills in robustly for the Centennial State here, even though Erik Messerschmidt's consistently charcoal-washed lensing suggests there's no magic hour in this unforgiving dystopia. This isn't a future to be prettified, and fair enough, but that impulse also falls in line with the film's stubbornly un-fun, eat-your-greens demeanor: Can't something here thrive rather than survive?

articles.title: Sandra Sá se conecta com o rap em EP motivacional, 'Indo pra dentro', que traz feats com King Saints e Davi Moraes | G1
articles.body:
Sandra Sá lança amanhã, quinta-feira, 27 de agosto, o EP 'Indo pra dentro' com sete músicas, sendo três inéditas e quatro regravações — Foto: Cristina Granato / Divulgação

♬ Em 1996, quando Sandra Sá lançou um dos mais coesos e sedutores álbuns de discografia que nem sempre esteve à altura da voz calorosa da cantora, “A lua sabe quem eu sou”, a artista carioca evocou a ancestralidade africana em uma das grandes músicas do disco, “Koo lei lei”, parceria da artista carioca com Kevin Mulligan.

É essa composição que encerrava o álbum “A lua sabe quem eu sou” – e que foi abafada na época pelo sucesso das gravações das músicas “Sozinho” (Peninha, 1996) e “Vamos viver” (Herbert Vianna, 1996) – que a cantora e compositora resgata, 30 anos depois, na faixa de abertura do EP “Indo pra dentro” em gravação de pegada afro que traz Marissol Mwaba e a rapper King Saints. “Não ando só / No meu sangue, carrego laços que dão os nós”, rima Saints no rap inserido em “Koo lei lei”.

Programado para ser lançado amanhã, quinta-feira, 27 de agosto, dia do 71º aniversário de Sandra Sá, com capa que expõe arte de Freddy Onirico, “Indo pra dentro” é disco situado na fronteira entre EP e álbum por reunir sete faixas gravadas com a alma funk soul da artista e com incursões pelo rap.

No disco, Sandra reforça os laços africanos em vibe positivista já traduzida no título, “Sou tão feliz” (Simone Malafaia, Sandra Sá, Bruno Gimenes e Patrícia Cândido), da música inédita que promove o EP “Indo pra dentro” em gravação que mistura soul, rock e rap – este novamente a cargo da rapper fluminense King Saints – e versos falados na voz grave de Sandra.

Com safra autoral de qualidade moderada, o EP “Indo pra dentro” soa como um chamado de união para a vida e para a luta – mote da música “Sobre viver [Cada linha]” (Sandra Sá, Simone Malafaia, Monica Odeh), outra inédita do disco.

Essa atmosfera de felicidade é acentuada pela regravação de “Dançando com a vida” (Sandra Sá, Zé Ricardo, Ana Lima e Gabriel O Pensador, 2000), música de outro álbum importante de Sandra, “Momentos que marcam demais” (2000). “Dançando com a vida” ganhou um toque de samba e versos falados na linha alto astral do EP, gravado com produção musical orquestrada pela própria Sandra Sá.

Parceria inédita de Sandra Sá com o guitarrista Davi Moraes e com Noé Ribeiro e Simone Malafaia, “Na pausa do compasso” tem batida funkeada e clima dançante à moda Black Rio, mas com beats contemporâneos. “Observa, absorva”, pedem Sandra e Davi, convidado da gravação, nos versos imperativos dessa faixa sobressalente no trio de músicas inéditas de “Indo pra dentro” pelo groove aliciante.

Música lançada pela cantora há 18 anos em gravação com os MCs Garrincha e Julinho, “Tem que acreditar” (Sandra Sá, Shayder, Julinho e Lidiane Madureira, 2008) é rebobinada no EP na mesma linha do funk com versos motivacionais que reforçam o traço de união sublinhado por Sandra nas letras desse repertório.

Fechando o EP “Indo pra dentro”, Sandra Sá regrava com certa vibração festiva a música “Movimento (Bagulho doido)”, parceria com Luiz Caldas e César Rasec apresentada pela cantora há 16 anos no álbum “Africanatividade – Cheiro de Brasil” (2010). A música é embasada pelo batuque miscigenado que tem a cara e o cheiro do Brasil.

Enfim, mesmo com baixo teor de novidade, o EP “Indo pra dentro” tem o mérito de trazer Sandra Sá – desde 2021 novamente sem o “de” que incorporara ao nome artístico em 1988 – de volta para o baile, agora em conexão com o rap, mas sem dissociar a cantora do funk e do soul, gêneros dos quais a artista é a primeira dama no Brasil.

articles.body:
A nona edição do Festival da Farinha em Cruzeiro do Sul , interior do Acre, inicia nesta quarta-feira (26) no Complexo Esportivo. A primeira noite tem muita música com artistas locais, show da cantora Mari Fernandez e o Concurso Melhor Prato derivado da Mandioca no estante de agricultura.

O Festival da Farinha ocorre todos os anos no município e tem como principal objetivo valorizar a cadeia produtiva da farinha de mandioca , principal produto da economia local. A festa segue até sábado (29).

As cantoras Mari Fernandez e Klessinha estão confirmadas para o festival. Mari Fernandez sobe ao palco às 23h. Klessinha se apresenta no sábado.

Além dos shows nacionais, o festival também terá apresentações de artistas locais. De acordo com o secretário municipal de Cultura, Flávio Rosas, foram credenciados 69 artistas.

Mari Fernandez e Klessinha são as primeiras atrações confirmadas para o 9º Festival da Farinha, em Cruzeiro do Sul — Foto: Divulgação

O evento também reúne apresentações culturais, shows e espaços para comercialização de produtos do agronegócio e de empreendedores da região do Juruá.

Em 2017, a farinha produzida em Cruzeiro do Sul recebeu o selo de Indicação Geográfica (IG) do Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial (INPI), que reconhece a qualidade e as características únicas do produto, referência na culinária da Região Norte.

Ao todo, 23 candidatos disputam os títulos de rei e rainha do Festival da Farinha, sendo 12 concorrentes ao posto de rei e 11 ao de rainha.

Os vencedores serão conhecidos na quinta-feira (27) e receberão premiações em dinheiro, além de produtos e serviços.

Na edição de 2025, os títulos ficaram com Mário Cesar e Carla Cristina, escolhidos após seletivas e semifinal. O príncipe foi Thiago Bernardo e a princesa, Kevila Silva. Os vencedores receberam cerca de R$ 12 mil em premiações, entre dinheiro e outros prêmios.

articles.title: AI-generated music barred from Australian charts after Madonna cover controversy
articles.summary: SYDNEY, Aug 26 (Reuters) - AI-generated music will be excluded from Australia's music charts starting this week, the country's peak music trade group said, f...
articles.body:
SYDNEY, Aug 26 (Reuters) - AI-generated music will be excluded from Australia's music charts starting this week, the country's peak music trade group said, ‌following controversy over an Australian DJ's cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" ‌topping local music charts.

The Australian Recording Industry Association, or ARIA, said on Tuesday that wholly AI-generated tracks ​would no longer be eligible for its popular ARIA Charts, although recordings that use generative AI in a supporting role would remain eligible.

A recording developed using generative AI will be eligible only if it is "substantially human made" and raises no concerns ‌around streaming or chart manipulation, ⁠ARIA said.

To distinguish AI-generated recordings from AI-assisted ones, ARIA said it would apply definitions from a labelling standard announced by the ⁠global music community in July.

Major global record labels have been seeking new licensing arrangements to protect their vast catalogues as AI-generated music grows in popularity and consumers increasingly ​struggle ​to distinguish it from human-composed songs.

"The ARIA ​charts will always remain a transparent ‌measurement of the music Australia consumes, but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent," ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said.

ARIA compiles Australia's most popular songs and albums in the ARIA Charts, which are released on Apple Music and Spotify every Friday.

Queensland-based ‌DJ Josh Fawaz's cover of Madonna's 1989 hit "Like ​a Prayer" became the most-played song on ​Australian radio and reached No. 4 ​on two ARIA charts in July. Some producers alleged that ‌generative AI had been used and ​that it was not ​initially disclosed.

Reuters could not immediately contact Fawaz for comment.

Responding to a music producer's criticism on Instagram in June, Fawaz said that although he used ​AI "as a tool, it's not ‌that deep", adding he had been releasing music long before AI ​and his focus was to provide his listeners "good music."

(Reporting by Renju ​Jose in Sydney; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.title: Paul McCartney Recalls Meeting Dolly Parton in 1970s Nashville, Shares Touching Tribute: ‘Such a Wonderful Woman’
articles.summary: McCartney shared the tribute amid the news of Parton’s death at 80 on Aug. 25
articles.body:
Paul McCartney shared heartfelt memories of meeting Dolly Parton at the Grand Ole Opry in the 1970s

McCartney praised Parton's unmatched talent, philanthropy, and business acumen in his emotional tribute following her death at 80 on Aug. 25

Parton's nephew announced her death months after she canceled her Las Vegas residency due to health challenges

Paul McCartney shared a heartfelt tribute to Dolly Parton following her death at 80 on Tuesday, Aug. 25.

McCartney, 84, shared two black-and-white photos taken by Jack Korn for The Tennesseean in 1974 in an Instagram post. The photos depict the pair of musicians first meeting, when McCartney and his late wife and Wings bandmate Linda McCartney visited Nashville to record the blues-rock influenced "Junior's Farm" and the country-tinged, fiddle-driven "Sally G."

In the photo, Parton can be seen greeting McCartney and his family, including daughters Heather and Mary.

"The magnificent star Dolly Parton has died and it is so sad," The Beatles alum began the tribute. "She was such a wonderful woman."

McCartney recalled first meeting the country icon at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, where she had been performing with Porter Wagoner . Parton would go on to pen her beloved emotional ballad " I Will Always Love You " about breaking from her musical partnership with Wagoner in 1974 in favor of pursuing a solo career.

"She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed," McCartney added of Parton. "Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."

The musician also described the "Jolene" singer as "a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world."

"There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song ' Let It Be ' and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honoured that she did it," McCartney added of her 2024 cover of The Beatles' 1970 hit for her album Rockstar. "I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents." "Thanks Dolly for the beautiful music you gave me and the whole world," he concluded. "We will always love you, god bless and rest in peace. You were the best."
