Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, announced his aunt's death in an Instagram video on Aug. 25, months after the cancellation of her 2025 residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas due to "health challenges."

Parton's team later announced in a statement that her death came shortly after she was diagnosed with cancer .

"Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly's unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact," the statement read in part. "After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones."

In a November 2025 cover story interview, Parton opened up to PEOPLE about her then-upcoming 80th birthday, and her hopes for the remainder of her life and career, including her dedication to philanthropy, namely through her Imagination Library.

"I'm at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on," Parton told PEOPLE at the time. "I'm proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people."

articles.title: Appreciation: Dolly Parton was special to the LGBTQ+ community. She showed us our country loves us
articles.summary: Dolly Parton loved LGBTQ+ people, and we loved her — in part because she showed us that our country still loves us too.
articles.body:
In a brief online elegy for Dolly Parton , with whom she'd worked on the women-empowering film "9 to 5," actor and famed liberal activist Jane Fonda made it a point to note that Parton cared about her queer fans.

"To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you," Fonda wrote. "You know that without me telling you."

Dolly meant something special to the LGBTQ+ community, in part because she represented an America where we are accepted — not just in big blue cities, but in one-room cabins in East Tennessee and in every rural, American-flag-flying corner of this big country.

Dolly was colorful and vivacious and unapologetic, and had more than a bit of drag queen in her. But she was also an unabashed ally with a country twang — a friend from the part of America where many queer people still instinctively put their guard up.

Of course, a country twang and queer acceptance can go hand in hand, and often do.

The Human Rights Campaign just last week cited a new U.S. Census Bureau analysis showing a record-high 12% of U.S. adults identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or gender diverse.

That's more than 25 million people, and they live all across the country. Many sound like Dolly. Many are surrounded by loving, supportive family too.

Yet it remained important, particularly as LGBTQ+ rights have come under increasing attack , that Dolly — big, beloved, down-home Dolly — had our back too.

She wrote and sang the Oscar-nominated song "Travelin' Thru" from the 2005 movie "Transamerica," about a transgender woman and her son. She collaborated with her goddaughter Miley Cyrus on "Rainbowland," a tribute to gay pride. And she made no secret of where she stood.

"I have some of everybody in my own immediate family and in my circle of employees. I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians," she said in 2023 . "I know and love them all, and I do not judge.… That's who they are. They cannot help that any more than I can help being Dolly Parton."

The LGBTQ+ community has watched in recent years as corporations and other supposed allies have backed away and gone quiet amid shifting politics and the Trump administration's war on diversity, equity and inclusion and the transgender community.

But not Dolly. We saw her stand her ground, next to us. And that meant something. Dolly showed that you can appeal to the whole of America without throwing LGBTQ+ people under the bus.

She showed that you can stand behind LGBTQ+ people without twisting into socially awkward or politically damaging positions, no matter your audience. Sometimes it just takes plain language about accepting everyone as they are.

She showed that holding onto faith, patriotism and the American way of life doesn't mean you can't also hold space for LGBTQ+ people to live their own happy lives.

She showed that we are all more alike than we are different, and that it's easier to see eye to eye when you aren't looking past one another.

Dolly showed that a country star and all-American icon, beloved as much in rural dive bars as big city queer clubs, could transcend the bogus narrative that LGBTQ+ lives are a political issue rather than a part of our collective humanity — and that all of us can too.

Dolly represented the America that LGBTQ+ people love and remain loyal to, the open-armed, diverse, compassionate, take-people-as-they-come version of America that is still all of ours to enjoy if we just work for it a little — just like Dolly did.

Dolly loved LGBTQ+ people, and we loved her — in part because she showed us that our country still loves us too.

articles.title: Dolly Parton Demonstrates How She Used Her Nails as an Instrument on the Set of “9 to 5” in Resurfaced 1981 Interview
articles.summary: “I’ve become famous for these nails,” Parton says in the clip
articles.body:
Dolly Parton used her acrylic nails to "get the rhythm" for the titular song on the set of 1980's 9 to 5

The country icon demonstrated the unique talent in a resurfaced interview clip from 1981

9 to 5 , which also starred Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, marked Parton's acting debut

Dolly Parton was a woman of many talents.

The country legend, who died on Aug. 25 at age 80 , utilized her creativity on the set of her acting debut, the 1980 movie 9 to 5 .

In an extended 1981 interview on Sacramento's KCRA 3 , Parton demonstrated how she would rub her acrylic nails together to "get the rhythm" for the film's titular theme song.

"Ladies and gentlemen, you are now viewing the newest instrument on the market," she joked as she "played" her long red nails.

Parton explained that when she was writing the song on the movie's set, she used her nails "just to get the rhythm when I wasn't close to my guitar."

"It worked out good," she added. "So now, I've become famous for these nails."

Parton elaborated on her acrylic nail playing in an episode of Apple Fitness+ Time to Walk experience in 2021, sharing that her nails are actually credited on the 9 to 5 soundtrack.

"I thought this sounded like a typewriter, and since that movie was about women in the workplace, I'd stand on the set, I'd watch things happening, I'd come up with little lines every day," she said of writing the song. "I'd go back to my hotel room at night and get my guitar and put it down on tape until after a couple months I had a song."

She added that her nails are featured on the official recording of the song. "And I played my nails—even on the record it says 'nails by Dolly'!" she said. "Anyhow, everybody makes me do this all the time, play this little sound [of her nails like a washboard]. Of course you have to have acrylic nails, your own nails won't do that. You gotta have falsies!"

The star also shared that she had been offered several movie roles prior to 9 to 5 but turned them all down.

Jane Fonda approached Parton about the project knowing the country star would help drive a Southern audience to a movie with a mission of drawing attention to equal pay for women. With Lily Tomlin already signed on and Fonda, the film had "two big stars, so if it does good, I can take my part of the credit, and if it don't do good, I can just blame it on them," Parton recalled with a laugh. "Nobody knew me in the movies anyway!"

articles.summary: Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards. The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight and elevate...
articles.body:
Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards.

The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight and elevate the craft of the Property Master by raising awareness, fostering collaboration among craft artisans, educating its members and inspiring future generations of Property Masters.

'Weapons,' 'Marty Supreme' and 'Hacks' Among 2026 MacGuffin Awards Nominees

'The Bear,' 'Oppenheimer' and More Win Property Masters Guild Awards

The honorees, recognized for their craftsmanship, service and dedication within the property department and the broader production community in entertainment, were announced Tuesday.

Castro will receive the Humanitarian Award for his 25-year-long career in the food industry as an executive chef, private chef, culinary instructor and restaurant owner. Over the past decade, he transitioned into food styling for film and television, including "This Is Us," "Westworld," "9-1-1," "Bel-Air," "Paradise" and "Barbie." He also founded Imagine Cookin, an in-home cooking class company for neurodivergent individuals.

Reilly is set to take home the Presidents Award for her career as a food stylist on titles like "Obi-Wan," "Rebel Moon" and "The Orville," as well as the culinary creations of "Grotesquerie" and drinkable blood for "American Horror Story."

Wilkinson will be awarded the Lifetime Achievement Award after 40 years in the property department. He served as the property master of "Titanic," "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom," "Who Framed Roger Rabbit," two James Bond films including "GoldenEye" and all eight of the original Harry Potter films.

"The MacGuffin Awards are about recognizing the people whose creativity, generosity and dedication help define our craft, both on set and beyond it," said PMG President Jeffrey Johnson. "Luis, Trish and Barry each represent a different and invaluable part of what makes the property community so special. Their careers and contributions reflect the skill, ingenuity and spirit that we are proud to celebrate."

articles.body: Sunny Deol-starrer 'Batwara 1947' arrived in theatres with considerable expectations, riding on the scale of the project, Aamir Khan's association as a producer and Preity Zinta's return to the big screen. However, the film has struggled to translate that anticipation into box office success and is currently well short of recovering its reported budget.Batwara 1947 Movie ReviewDirected by Rajkumar Santoshi, the film opened with Rs 5.75 crore on Day 1 before witnessing a strong jump on Saturday, when it collected Rs 13.50 crore. The momentum did not sustain, with Sunday's collection dropping to Rs 7.25 crore and the first Monday bringing in just Rs 2 crore. 'Batwara 1947' eventually wrapped up its opening week with Rs 33.60 crore.The film has remained subdued in its second week as well. It added Rs 75 lakh on the second Friday, followed by Rs 1.15 crore on Saturday and Rs 1.30 crore on Sunday. The weekday collections have been particularly weak, with Day 11 bringing in only Rs 35 lakh. On the second Tuesday, Day 12, the film earned Rs 55 lakh.With these collections, 'Batwara 1947' has taken its India net total to Rs 37.70 crore. Given that the film was reportedly mounted on a budget of around Rs 120 crore, its current theatrical performance points towards a significant loss.The film's underwhelming run has also prompted trade analysts to examine why it failed to connect with audiences despite positive elements. Trade analyst Taran Adarsh recently shared his assessment with Bollywood Hungama, admitting that the film's failure surprised him.âWhat has really surprised me is why this film has not worked. In my opinion, it was a well-made film. I genuinely felt that the emotions between Shabana Azmi and Sunny Deol were very well captured on screen. The performances were of a very high order, while Rajkumar Santoshiâs direction was top-notch. The finale was very gripping. I am still unable to figure out and put a finger on why the film did not work.âAdarsh also addressed the argument that the audience may have expected Sunny Deol to deliver the kind of high-octane performance associated with his recent successes.He continued, âA lot of people told me, and I even read online, that Sunnyâs image is associated with films like Gadar (2001), Gadar 2 (2023), Jaat (2025), etc., where he is seen screaming and indulging in action. Nevertheless, it was a well-made film that did not get its due.âDespite its strong cast, experienced director and considerable production scale, 'Batwara 1947' has therefore failed to find the kind of audience response needed to turn its theatrical run into a commercial success.Meanwhile, it may now end its theatrical run with the release of Yash starrer Toxic, which will occupy major screens across the country.Give your child the gift of confidence! articles.title: Billy Ray Cyrus breaks silence on Dolly Parton's death with nod to rumored '90s affair
articles.summary: Billy Ray Cyrus has broken his silence in the wake of country superstar Dolly Parton's death with a moving tribute. See details.
articles.body:
Billy Ray Cyrus has broken his silence in the wake of country superstar Dolly Parton 's death with a moving tribute, even touching on the duo's rumored affair in the '90s when he was just breaking into the mainstream.

Dolly passed away on August 25 – which is also Billy Ray's birthday – at age 80, following a brief battle with cancer . She had dealt with several health issues in the last year of her life, particularly since the loss of her husband, Carl Dean , in March 2025.

Billy Ray took to Instagram to pay tribute to his late friend, who served as the godmother of his daughter, Miley Cyrus.

"I have so many moments and memories with Dolly, it's hard to know where to start. Like every little boy, I grew up loving Dolly Parton. She was a part of our lives, on our TVs, right in our living rooms," he wrote, alongside a carousel of photos of the pair.

"In 1992, I'll never forget walking into her dressing room to apologize for all the tabloid stories which claimed I was having an affair with her. In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said, 'Honey, this trash sells records!'" he continued.

"Dolly recently sent me a beautiful message, telling me she loved me with her whole heart. I will always love her in the same way…with my whole heart…and I always will," Billy concluded.

Learn more about Dolly's passing below...

Billy and Dolly met back in the '90s, and they became close friends after touring together.

"When Billy had the big song, 'Achy Breaky Heart,' well, we toured together. I was on tour, and then Billy toured with me, and so that's how we just got to be good friends, because he's a Kentucky boy, I'm from Tennessee," she shared on The Howard Stern Show .

Dolly Parton's heartbreaking cause of death revealed

Miley Cyrus' 'terrible habit' she learned from Dolly Parton, leading to new Hannah Montana special

Dolly Parton's legacy of kindness in her own words

Billy Ray asked Dolly to be Miley's godmother before her birth in 1992. "He said…'We're having a girl, and you've got to be her godmother!' And I said, 'Well, I'd be honored,'" the "Jolene" singer recalled on the show.

"So actually, Miley and I took over from there. We've just stayed very, very close through the years…I love Miley. She's my little sweetheart. I've known her since before she was born, actually."

Billy Ray shared insight into Dolly and Miley's close bond on AXS TV , revealing that the pair "actually just fell in love".

"Like it was kindred spirits. That sounds silly, but they were absolute. You could just feel it from the second they met. It was two peas in a pod."

Similarly, Miley has sung her godmother's praises time and again, including in an interview with TIME . "Dolly is not only my idol because of her incomparable career – she's also my role model because of her steadfast morals and values. At her core, she is the definition of a humanitarian," the "Flowers" singer wrote.

"Though she created an identity that she downplays as being built on wigs, lots of gingham and silicone, the foundation for this empire is actually her honesty, truth and her faith," Miley continued.

"People look to Dolly for guidance, and she knows that. She wears that responsibility with the same grace and pride she rocks a two-piece Nudie suit. She recognizes how impactful her choices will be as one of the most iconic and powerful voices in country music, and she leaves no one behind."

The Grammy winner concluded: "She's even better than your sparkliest dreams. She may be my fairy godmother, but I think she's that to everyone else too. I am happy to share her with the world."

articles.title: Dolly Parton's final words take on heartbreaking new meaning after her death at 80
articles.summary: The country legend spoke candidly about her late husband Carl Dean, her health struggles and the dreams
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was still dreaming about the future just four days before her death at the age of 80. The country music legend died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday, August 25, following a brief battle with cancer , her team confirmed.

But in what would become her final interview, published by People on August 21, Dolly remained characteristically optimistic, speaking about the projects she still hoped to complete and insisting that, despite ongoing health struggles, she was "still working."

The poignancy of her words is even greater in light of her death just four days later. "You know me, as I've often said, I've dreamed myself into a corner and I still have so many things I want to achieve," she said, adding that she planned to keep working for as long as she could.

Dolly Parton's heartbreaking cause of death revealed

Who will inherit Dolly Parton's staggering $450 million fortune?

Dolly had been candid about experiencing health problems in the months leading up to her death, which had forced her to cancel several appearances and ultimately abandon plans for a Las Vegas residency.

In her final interview, the Jolene singer revealed that some of those problems had been neglected while she devoted herself to caring for her beloved husband, Carl Dean, before his death in March 2025.

"As I've shared in video messages throughout the past year, I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn't pay attention to when I was watching over Carl," she told the publication.

See the announcement of Dolly's death below...

Dolly acknowledged that it had been a difficult period, but typically refused to dwell on it. "It's not like I haven't been through hard times with my health," she said.

The singer also joked that speculation surrounding her condition had been amplified by the modern news cycle and social media, before making it clear she had no intention of quietly retiring. "Seriously, though, even though I'm still healin', I'm still workin'!" she said.

It was an outlook Dolly had maintained even as concern for her wellbeing intensified. In October 2025, following a public request for prayers from her sister Freida, she reassured worried fans in a video: "I don't think God is through with me, and I ain't done working."

Far from contemplating the end of her extraordinary seven-decade career, Dolly was still planning what came next.

She was working on the Life of Many Colors museum in Nashville, her SongTeller Hotel and her Broadway musical, Dolly: A True Original Musical, alongside a string of other ventures.

She also spoke excitedly about Cup of Ambition Coffee, a collaboration inspired by one of the most famous lyrics from her 1980 hit 9 to 5. The idea had been in the making for more than four decades, she revealed, adding that "some dreams take longer to come to life than others."

Even performing remained in Dolly's plans, although she admitted her days of traditional touring were behind her. "I definitely plan to do special performances in the future, but I won't tour anymore like I used to," she explained.

In typical Dolly fashion, she had even found a humorous solution, revealing that she was exploring the possibility of an avatar-based show in Nashville that could allow audiences to experience a Dolly Parton performance without requiring her to physically take to the stage. "I won't have to show up in person, but I still get paid!" she joked. "Sounds like a pretty good deal to me."

Dolly's enduring love for husband Carl Dean

Behind Dolly's determination to continue was an intensely difficult period in her personal life. Carl died in March 2025 at the age of 82, bringing to an end one of showbusiness' longest and most famously private marriages.

The couple first met outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville in 1964, on the day an 18-year-old Dolly arrived in the city to pursue her dreams.

They married two years later and remained together for almost six decades, despite Carl largely choosing to stay away from the spotlight that surrounded his wife.

After his death, Dolly paid tribute to the man who had quietly remained by her side throughout her extraordinary rise from rural Tennessee to global superstardom.

"Carl and I spent many wonderful years together," she wrote. "Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years." She added: "Thank you for your prayers and sympathy."

The loss had a profound effect on Dolly, who later admitted that learning how to live without her husband was a significant adjustment. Her final interview makes clear that caring for Carl had also taken precedence over her own health.

Dolly's death was announced by her nephew Bryan Seaver, who also served as her longtime head of security. Her representatives subsequently confirmed that the music legend died following a "brief battle with cancer." A small private service will be held for her immediate family, with fans encouraged to donate to her beloved Imagination Library in lieu of flowers.

In a statement, her team remembered the singer's extraordinary life and the warmth that made her as beloved away from the stage as she was on it. "A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see," the statement read, adding that Dolly would remain an inspiration through her music, songwriting, "wit, warmth and kindness."

Her death came after a career spanning seven decades in which she became one of the most recognizable entertainers in the world, selling more than 100 million records and writing thousands of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You.

Out of respect, we have withdrawn the said advertisement from all media. Wish you all the love & positivity this festive season!âKriti, meanwhile, had argued that festivals are defined by their emotions and traditions rather than clothing. articles.title: Nuevo descenso térmico a las puertas del fin de semana: una masa de aire polar llega a España
articles.standfirst: La inestabilidad vuelve a ser protagonista
articles.summary: La inestabilidad vuelve a ser protagonista
articles.body: El mes de agosto, muy especialmente la segunda quincena, se está caracterizando por sus continuos cambios y las diferencias térmicas respecto a sus primeros días. Tanto es así que una masa de aire polar va a irrumpir en la Península en las próximas horas y, justo a las puertas del fin de semana, las temperaturas van a caer en picado en varios puntos del territorio nacional. Al parecer, la entrada de una borrasca derivará en una especie de tregua de lluvias durante este miércoles, 26 de agosto, pero que comenzará a afectar a España a partir del jueves, 27 de agosto. Será entonces cuando se noten sus efectos y poco a poco se desplomen las temperaturas. Las lluvias comenzarán a caer por el oeste y el noroeste de la Península y se irán extendiendo hacia el interior, donde también podrían producirse algunas tormentas. A partir del viernes, 28 de agosto, esas precipitaciones alcanzarán el punto mediterráneo e irán a menos en la parte oeste. Lo más notable será el bajón térmico, que provocará situaciones como por ejemplo en ciudades como Madrid, donde se pasará rápidamente de 29 a 25 grados de máxima. En Albacete esa diferencia será aún más grande, con 34 grados en la jornada de este miércoles a 28 en las siguientes 48 horas. En Murcia habrá una diferencia de hasta 10 grados, esto es, de 37 a 27 grados. Las máximas serán de apenas 16 grados en ciudades como Lugo, mientras otros puntos como León o Burgos se moverán en torno a los 18 y 22 grados respectivamente. Además, las mínimas serán menores a los 10 grados. Eso sí, durante el fin de semana se producirá un nuevo repunte, según los informes, y las temperaturas volverán a ascender por encima de los 30 ºC y todo apunta a que se mantendrá en los primeros días de septiembre.

articles.title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
articles.summary: The much-loved country singer-songwriter in her own words, following her death aged 80.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the much-loved US singer-songwriter who has died at the age of 80 , was known for her pearls of wisdom and humour as well as her music.

She regularly offered her perceptive and witty insights about life, music, fame and equal rights.

Here are some of her most memorable quotes from down the years:

"The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

"I always just thought if you see somebody without a smile, give 'em yours!"

"I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one."

"Don't get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life."

"Sometimes, what would look like to be my biggest mistakes turn out to be my biggest blessings."

"I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."

"It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy."

"You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."

"I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."

"I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."

"My dream was always to make as many people happy as I could in this life."

"I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."

"I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."

How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs Published 9 hours ago

How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millions Published 14 hours ago

Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millions

'Iâll think of you each step of the way' - Taylor Swift leads tributes after Dolly Parton dies aged 80

"If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"

"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb - and I'm not blonde either."

"It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."

"People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don't know, I'm never there."

"If I see something sagging, bagging and dragging, I'm going to nip it, tuck it, and suck it."

"I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."

"I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"

"I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."

Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."

"I'm very real where it counts, and that's inside."

"They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."

"I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."

"I don't want to be a star if I have no life."

Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."

"I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

"When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".

Journalist: "What would be her funeral song?" Dolly: "I don't know - but I won't be singing it!"

"Yes, I support gay marriage. They have every right to be as miserable as straight people."

"And of course black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!"

"I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."

"It's a good thing I was born a girl, otherwise I'd be a drag queen."

In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."

She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.

"You are terrific, and remember... I will always love you."

articles.title: Dolly Parton for beginners: How the Queen of Country wrote the playbook for Taylor Swift
articles.summary: Explore how Dolly Parton shaped the music industry and influenced artists like Taylor Swift, breaking barriers in country and pop music with her extraordinary talent, business acumen, and cultural impact.
articles.body: Dolly Parton’s status as the Queen of Country never quite explained the scale of her influence. A better measure came from Marshall Mathers, better known as Eminem, who after her death shared a handwritten note she had sent him following his induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Parton had congratulated him, admitted she knew little about rap and told him that he was “very special” and touched people in ways he probably did not even realise.Eminem’s response said even more about her reach. “Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense.” It was an unlikely exchange on paper: the blonde, rhinestone-clad queen of Nashville and the enfant terrible of Detroit rap. Yet that was precisely the point. Dolly’s influence had long escaped the boundaries of country music.After her death on August 25 at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer, the tributes stretched across generations and genres. Taylor Swift said a world without Dolly did not feel “possible, real, or right”. Paul McCartney, Jane Fonda, Kacey Musgraves, Reba McEntire and Carrie Underwood were among those who mourned her. Eminem Stanned her.Dolly had stopped being merely a country star decades ago. She had become something closer to an American institution.The rags before the rhinestonesDolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, the fourth of 12 children, and grew up in a one-room cabin in Locust Ridge in the Great Smoky Mountains. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, worked as a farmer and labourer and could not read or write. Her mother, Avie Lee, filled the house with songs and stories.Music became Dolly’s exit route. She was performing on local radio and television as a child, writing songs while other children were still learning multiplication tables, and appeared at the Grand Ole Opry at 13. The day after graduating from high school in 1964, she left for Nashville.“Coat of Many Colors”, one of her greatest songs, tells the story of a coat her mother stitched together from scraps. Dolly is proud of it until her classmates laugh at her.That is the trick in so many Parton songs. The language is simple, but the emotional equation is not. “Coat of Many Colors” is about maternal love, but it is also about class, humiliation and the moment a child discovers that other people can make poverty shameful.Porter Wagoner and the great escapeDolly’s breakthrough came in 1967 when Porter Wagoner recruited her for The Porter Wagoner Show. Wagoner was already a major country star; Dolly was the newcomer. Their television partnership made her famous, produced hit duets and gave her the platform from which her solo career could grow.Eventually, however, the protégé outgrew the mentor.Dolly wanted to leave. Wagoner did not want her to go. So she wrote him a song.“I Will Always Love You” is now inseparable from Whitney Houston, whose 1992 version became one of the biggest singles in pop history. Dolly’s original is very different: quieter, smaller and more intimate. More importantly, it was not fundamentally a romantic breakup song. It was a farewell to Wagoner, telling a man she loved and respected that affection did not require permanent professional dependence.Then there was “Jolene”. Instead of attacking the beautiful woman she fears may steal her man, Dolly’s narrator begs her. She admires Jolene almost as much as she fears her. Jealousy, vulnerability, fascination and desperation coexist inside one of country music’s simplest melodies.How do you become the Queen of Country?Dolly’s distinction was that she made country portable.Her early catalogue established her as one of Nashville’s great storytellers. “Joshua” gave her a solo No. 1. “The Bargain Store” turned emotional damage into the metaphor of second-hand goods still worth buying. “Light of a Clear Blue Morning” captured the feeling of emerging from professional turmoil.Then “Here You Come Again” pushed her decisively towards pop in 1977. She carried the accent, the hair, the humour and the Tennessee mythology with her.In 1980 came 9 to 5, opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Dolly played a secretary dealing with a sexist boss and also wrote the title song, turning the click of her acrylic nails into part of the rhythm.“9 to 5” became a No. 1 pop hit and a working-woman anthem. The casting was almost too perfect. Dolly had spent years being underestimated because she looked like exactly the kind of woman powerful men were conditioned not to take seriously. Now she was playing one.Three years later, “Islands in the Stream”, her duet with Kenny Rogers, became another enormous crossover success. By then Dolly could move between Nashville, Hollywood and mainstream pop without ever appearing to be visiting any of them.Dolly IncThe most revealing Dolly Parton story may involve a song she did not allow Elvis Presley to record.Elvis wanted “I Will Always Love You”. His manager, Colonel Tom Parker, demanded half the publishing rights. Dolly refused. She kept the song, a decision vindicated when Whitney Houston turned it into a global phenomenon nearly two decades later.This is where the road from Dolly Parton to Taylor Swift becomes particularly interesting.Swift’s battle over her masters involved a different part of music copyright, but the philosophy is remarkably similar: fame is useful, ownership is better. Understand what you have created, understand what rights attach to it and do not assume the men in suits know more about the value of your work than you do.Dolly understood that lesson when female performers were often treated as voices and faces attached to songs, contracts and catalogues controlled by other people.Dollywood turned her East Tennessee roots into a major tourist business. Dolly was a brand before celebrity branding became an industry.The woman behind DollyFor someone who made herself visually impossible to ignore, Dolly protected her private life with astonishing success.She met Carl Dean outside a Nashville laundromat on her first day in the city. They married in 1966 and remained together until his death in March 2025, nearly 59 years later.Dean wanted virtually nothing to do with show business. While Dolly became one of the most photographed women in the world, her husband largely stayed away from cameras, premieres and interviews.They had no children. Dolly instead became famously close to nieces, nephews and her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.The audience got Dolly Parton. Carl Dean got Dolly.From Dolly to TaylorThe line from Parton to Taylor Swift is not that Swift copied Dolly. It is that Dolly helped widen the space in which later female stars could operate.Both arrived in Nashville young. Both insisted that songwriting was central to their identity. Both crossed from country into pop. Both turned apparently conventional femininity into something commercially powerful rather than something for which they had to apologise. Both understood that control of intellectual property mattered. And both faced the strange assumption that a woman cannot simultaneously be a serious artist and an exceptionally clever businessperson.Dolly’s response to that problem was particularly ingenious.She exaggerated everything.The wigs got bigger. The heels got higher. The clothes got tighter. She joked constantly about cosmetic surgery and her appearance. Instead of trying to persuade people not to see a “dumb blonde”, she gave them the most spectacular dumb-blonde costume imaginable and then quietly owned the songs, the publishing and eventually much of the business underneath the spectacle.That is perhaps her largest contribution to the women who followed her. She showed that femininity did not have to be surrendered to acquire authority. Her influence also travelled in less obvious directions. Beyoncé could rework “Jolene”, Miley Cyrus could inherit the mixture of country roots and pop spectacle, and Swift could turn songwriting ownership into part of her public mythology because Dolly had already demonstrated that a female star did not need to choose between commercial calculation, humour, glamour and artistic seriousness.The beginner’s playlistIf you know Dolly but not the music, start with “Coat of Many Colors” for the storyteller; “Jolene” for vulnerability; “I Will Always Love You” for the songwriter and businesswoman; “The Bargain Store” for her gift for metaphor; “Here You Come Again” for the crossover star; “Light of a Clear Blue Morning” for independence; “9 to 5” for the working-woman icon; and “Islands in the Stream” for Dolly at maximum mainstream wattage.Then go deeper into “Joshua”, “Love Is Like a Butterfly”, “Two Doors Down”, “Old Flames Can’t Hold a Candle to You” and her Trio recordings with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris.In 1995, partly inspired by her father’s inability to read, Dolly launched the Imagination Library, which mails free books to young children. It eventually expanded across several countries and distributed hundreds of millions of books.That may be why the mourning extended so far beyond Nashville.Dolly Parton spent a lifetime looking artificial and being remarkably real. She escaped poverty without disowning where she came from, escaped Nashville’s restrictions without abandoning country, crossed into Hollywood without giving up songwriting and turned a deliberately exaggerated image into armour.Most importantly, she understood the difference between fame and power. Fame was having everybody recognise the hair. Power was owning the song.Give your child the gift of confidence! Claim your exclusive TOI Masterclass spot today!

articles.title: Dolly Parton's life in her own words: from Smoky Mountains poverty to country music immortality
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's life in her own words reveals her Smoky Mountains childhood, faith, marriage to Carl Dean and her views on aging and what comes after.
articles.body: Country music icon Dolly Parton died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday at 80 years old. Parton's team shared a statement with Fox News Digital on Tuesday night and confirmed that she died after a "brief battle with cancer." Parton's death sparked mourning across the world. Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard." Throughout the span of her career, which ignited as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton always shared what mattered most to her – her Tennessee upbringing, her faith, her beloved husband, Carl Dean, and family. Below is a look at Parton's life, in her own words, over the years. DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80 Smoky Mountains upbringing Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child and started writing songs at a young age. In 2015, Parton told Entertainment Tonight that her upbringing shaped who she became in her adult years. "I think my childhood made me everything I am today. I would trade nothing for being brought up in the Great Smoky Mountains. I’ve never been ashamed of my people no matter how poor or dirty we might have been," she said at the time. Parton added, "I’ve always loved being from where I am, and having the folks that I’ve had." During an interview with Rolling Stone in January, Parton shed a little more light on her poor childhood and said that her mother would make her clothes out of "feed sacks or scraps." "We didn’t have anything. Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps," she said. Parton was one of 12 children. Her parents were Robert Lee Parton Sr., known as Lee, a sharecropper and construction worker, and Avie Lee Caroline Parton, who raised their family. Dolly's faith Parton was very outspoken throughout her life about her Christian faith. During an interview with Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that her faith impacted everything she did. GRAMMY-NOMINATED SINGER ANNE WILSON SAYS SPEAKING ABOUT JESUS COST HER OPPORTUNITIES, BUT SHE WON'T BACK DOWN "My faith impacts everything I do because I do believe that, through God, all things are possible," she said at the time. "I always ask God to bless everything that I do and the people that I work with and to bring all the right things and right people into my life and to take the wrong ones out." WATCH: Dolly Parton discusses the important role faith plays in her life She added, "My spirituality has been a guiding light in my life and my strength, really, in my creative energy." On the "WorkLife with Adam Grant" Ted Talk series in 2022, Parton shared that her religious beliefs were instilled in her at a young age. "My grandpa was preacher. My mom was very religious, very spiritual. So I learned all the good lessons about loving your neighbor as yourself and judge not lest you be judged. Through God, all things are possible," she said. WILLIE ROBERTSON'S FAITH-BASED ADVICE THAT'S KEPT HIS 34-YEAR MARRIAGE TO WIFE KORIE STRONG WATCH: Dolly Parton: ‘I pray a lot and God's been really good to me' Fox News looked back on Parton's history speaking about God in public. "I pray a lot and God's been really good to me," she said in March. In 2018, Parton said that music is "everything to me." "It's my gift, it's my joy, it's my job," she continued. Marriage to Carl Dean Parton met Carl Dean outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville on her first day in the city in 1964, when she was 18. They married two years later, on May 30, 1966, and remained together for nearly six decades until Dean’s death in 2025. After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs. DOLLY PARTON'S HUSBAND, CARL DEAN, DEAD AT 82 "I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes." "I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said. Also, shortly after Dean's death, Parton told People that she would always keep him close to her heart. "Ours is a great old love story. Most people don’t stay that close that long. That’s a loss. Nobody can ever know that unless you’ve experienced it yourself. He will always be in my heart and in my memories," she said. Speaking to Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that part of the reason she believes their marriage lasted as long as it did was because she kept it private. WATCH: Dolly Parton shares the secret to her long-time marriage "The fact that he's not in show business at all, so we're not in competition on that. We don't have to deal with it. He's kind of a homebody. He loves working on the farm. He loves workin' on his tractors and his trucks and all that. He was in asphalt paving for years, and then he went into kinda doin' some real estate. But he don't wanna be in the spotlight, but he's very proud of and for me," she said at the time. "When I first won an award, when we first married in '66... he just started taking clothes off before we even got out of the building. Before we got to the car, he had that bowtie off from that tuxedo. Had that shirt, jacket off, and he said, 'I want you to be successful. Do whatever you want to do, but leave me out of this. I ain't doing any more of these things, so don't ask me.' So I never did it," Parton said. Shortly after Dead died, Parton told The Associated Press that she "truly believe[s] that I’m going to see him again someday." Dolly's legacy Parton built a seven-decade career as a singer, songwriter, actress, author, businesswoman and philanthropist, winning 11 Grammy Awards and becoming one of country music’s most enduring stars. Beyond music, she created Dollywood, founded the Imagination Library and brought her larger-than-life personality to films including "9 to 5" and "Steel Magnolias." In 2025, Parton spoke to People about how she was able to not only maintain a country music career, but crossover to Hollywood successfully and find the time for her charitable efforts. "I don’t try to tell other people how to do it, how to be, but I know who I am. I’m a star to everybody but me. I’m just a working girl. I always just say that I’m a workhorse that looks like a show horse," she said at the time. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I’m at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on. I’m proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people," Parton added. In 2022, Parton said part of the reason she found the time to do the things she loved was because she didn't sleep much. "I don’t need a whole lot of sleep," the singer insisted to Insider. "I go to bed pretty early, but even if I’ve been up late – it’s just kind of like a little clock inside of me that says, ‘It’s 3 o’clock!’" "I do some of my best work there, but I get enough sleep. I don’t require as much sleep as a lot of other people do. That’s kind of a Parton family trait," she continued. Parton's stance on aging After Parton turned 77 in 2023, she spoke to Insider about how she viewed getting older. The singer said she's come to terms with the idea that "wisdom comes with age, and you can't stop the aging process, nor the numbers." DOLLY PARTON SAYS SHE’D ‘RATHER BE’ IN HER 70S THAN BE YOUNG AGAIN: ‘I MEAN THIS FROM THE BOTTOM OF MY HEART’ "Honestly — and I mean this from the bottom of my heart — when I see young people today and I see what they're going to have to go through, especially in this day and time, I would honestly rather be this age than that age," Parton explained. The legendary singer acknowledged she's no different from "everyone (who) would like to stay 35 forever," but she doesn't spend her life thinking about her age and doesn't let it get in the way of her doing what she wants. "The way I live, the way I work, the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count," Parton said. "I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything." "As long as I stay healthy, the numbers shouldn't matter. I don't feel my age, I don't work my age, I don't think my age and, hopefully, I don't look my age," she noted. "I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything." Just before her 80th birthday this year, Parton told People that she felt like she was "just getting started." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "If you allow yourself to get old, you will. People say, ‘How come you don’t seem to get old?’ I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old,’" she said. "I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about," she told the outlet. What Dolly believed came after death In 2019, Parton shared rare comments on what she believed would happen after she died during an episode of the "Dolly Parton's America" podcast. "As far as what happens after we go on, like I say, I’m no saint so I’m hoping just as a Christian faith person, that we go on to a greater thing. I believe that we’re all part of that great divine plan, and I’m hoping to get on up there, and do some more writing, and singing, and playing with those golden harps, and write some more songs, and have my own mansion, and walk them golden streets of glory, and keep doing it forever and ever and ever. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "So I’m going to get in the angel band, for sure. I want to play in the angel band and I want to maybe play the harp up there. I don’t know," she said. On the podcast, Parton said that she "kind of" believed in reincarnation and was "open to things." "You just hope and you have faith. That’s what faith is. But I believe that it’s going to be better. I think it’s not the end of me. I don’t think it’s the end of any of us. I think we’re recycled and if nothing else, we just go back into that great flow of divine energy, and hopefully we can spread ourselves around in other wonderful ways. That’s what I hope," Parton said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.body: Dolly Parton was one of the most beloved figures in the entertainment industry. She started from almost nothing, one of 12 siblings, and ended up becoming one of the biggest icons in the industry. Todayâs inspiring quote of the day from the beloved icon is all about understanding that there is a real difference between things that you wish for and things that you dream about. One means that you are only thinking about the things that you do not have, whereas the other means that you have already taken the crucial first step towards your goal by clearly imagining that you are already living it.Dolly Partonâs quote of the day reads, "Be careful. Do not confuse dreams with wishes. There is a difference. Dreams are where you visualize yourself being successful at what's important to you to accomplish. Now, dreams build convictions because you work hard to pay the price to make sure that they come true. Wishes are hoping good things will happen to you, but there's no fire in your gut that causes you to put everything forth, you know, to overcome all the obstacles. So you have to dream more and never, ever, ever blame somebody else if it doesn't happen.âWhat does the quote mean?Dolly Parton said these words on May 8, 2009, when she was delivering her commencement address to the graduating class of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. She was awarded an honorary doctorate of humane letters there.Partonâs quote is all about redefining the concept of "dreaming" by stripping away its passive connotations. Instead, she says that dreaming means that you are already stepping towards your goals by dreaming about them, by imagining yourself in a successful place; however, she also defines that wishing for something should not be mistaken for dreaming.Parton stressed in her quote that dreaming is a way of visualizing yourself being successful. A wish lacks clarity and target focus; a dream creates a concrete mental destination. When you clearly picture the goal, you establish the starting line for what your actions must achieve. Wishing, however, does not come with any strength or cost; it is simply something that you hoped you had, or you hoped was true. However, at the end of the day, it does not mean that you are taking action towards your goals.A wish costs nothing at the end of the day, which is why it brings nothing. However, a dream requires you to pay the price up front through labor, effort, missed comforts, adjustments, and sustained focus.The final line, "Never, ever, ever blame somebody else if it doesn't happen," provides a base for the entire quote. Blame is the ultimate hallmark of a wish; it assumes someone else was responsible for your success or at least bringing you close to your goals rather than yourself. By taking total ownership of your dreams, you surrender the right to make excuses. You take full control of your actions and your wants, and you must understand the differences between your own wishes and your dreams.All about Dolly Parton and her legacyDolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, in Sevier County, Tennessee. She was the fourth of 12 children. She was born to Robert Lee Parton Sr. and Avie Lee Owens Parton and, from an early age, lived in a middle-class household. They lived in a small cabin near the Great Smoky Mountains, and while her mother was a homemaker, her father used to work as a tobacco farmer and construction worker.Parton was interested in music from a young age and started off by performing in churches and learning music from her relatives. Over the years, she often credited her uncle, Bill Owens, as one of the biggest and most influential mentors in her life, who helped her find her footing in the industry. The country music singer first came in front of the camera when she was nine years old on âThe Cas Walker Show.'She was 18 when she moved to Nashville to pursue her career in music more professionally. She first started booking projects as a songwriter, with many of the songs that she had written reaching the top of the music charts at the time. She released her first song, âDumb Blonde,' in 1967, which was followed by her debut album, âHello, I'm Dolly.âOver the course of her career, Parton released a total of 49 solo studio albums, 4 collaborative albums, 9 live albums, and 6 soundtrack albums. Her last album was released in 2023, titled âRockstar.â All of her songs were inspired by her everyday life and events and were big hits amongst the masses. To date, Parton was referred to as a legend in the music industry and will be remembered by millions of people across the world.Give your child the gift of confidence! articles.summary: Al omitir la responsabilidad de Marruecos y del jefe de inteligencia marroquí
articles.body: Desde el pasado mes de julio, España se enfrenta a una grave crisis migratoria en la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta. Un mes después, se sigue discutiendo sobre el conocimiento o no de que esto pudiese suceder, con dos versiones que se anteponen entre sí. Margarita Robles, ministra de defensa, reconoció los avisos del CNI acerca de un evento similar al que acabó ocurriendo, mientras que Grande-Marlaska, de Interior, defiende que no se anticipó la gravedad de lo ocurrido. El periodista Antonio Maestre ha dado su punto de vista al respecto en la última emisión de ‘Al Rojo Vivo’, en laSexta, dándole a los dos ministros su parte de razón, pero afirmando que también ambos mienten. “Las dos versiones son compatibles, porque hubo siete avisos antes del 31 de julio por parte del CNI, ningún informe escrito. Hubo siete avisos y esos avisos en ningún caso anticiparon la dimensión de lo que ocurrió el 31 de julio. Se avisó de que estaba ocurriendo o que iba a ocurrir un evento de gente nadando, en ningún caso se avisó de que iban a pasar 80.000 personas”, iniciaba en su opinión. Seguidamente, el colaborador de laSexta explica que cada uno elige la versión más favorable a los intereses de su ministerio: “Pero el problema está en que aquí eso no tendría que haber ocurrido, tendría que haber un relato unificado”, prosigue echando la culpa en este sentido a la inacción desde presidencia. “Un relato que además es compatible con ambas versiones. Pero como Pedro Sánchez no sabemos dónde está, pues no ha podido darlo, porque es el único que podía haber dado un relato unificado que contara la verdad”, explica. A continuación, el periodista ha señalado que ambos mienten en una parte: “Ninguno señala a Marruecos, porque ambos saben que el jefe de la inteligencia marroquí al que Marlaska condecoró, Abdelatif Hammouchi, estaba detrás de esto”.
